subtopic: SUGGESTED PROHIBITION OF ENTRY INTO CANADA OF MAGAZINES "KEN" AND "LIFE"

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROHIBITION OF ENTRY INTO CANADA OF MAGAZINES "KEN" AND "LIFE"
speechtext: I should like to direct the attention of the government to the fact that the magazine Ken is again being sold on the news stands; and, since its subject matter has not been improved at all, I should like to know why the ban on this magazine has been lifted.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: SUGGESTED PROHIBITION OF ENTRY INTO CANADA OF MAGAZINES "KEN" AND "LIFE"
speechtext: The magazine in question was banned, that is entry was prohibited, some time ago because it published a cartoon which was offensive and which the Department of National Revenue considered came within the terms of the provisions of the Customs Tariff relating to such publications. The customary period of prohibition is for six issues. The issues that followed were not objectionable from the point of view of the Department of National Revenue. Not only was that the case; the publishers of Ken gave an undertaking to the government to desist from publishing material of the type they had published previously, or at least on that one occasion, and also published an editorial in which they expressed their regret. Since that time I am not aware that the publication has contained anything that could possibly be construed as of a seditious or treasonable nature. For that reason there appears to be no ground for prohibiting the magazine from entering Canada.

CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN AD IAN PACIFIC ACT, 1933 *-COMPENSATION OF EMPLOYEES AFFECTED BY COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT
The house resumed from Friday, May 26, consideration in committee of Bill No. 138, to amend the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933-Mr. Howe-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On the schedule-paragraph 2.

What would be regarded as the beginning of the term of employment of persons who had been laid off because of cooperative measures after 1933, and were again taken on? Would they be given credit for the years of employment before the first lay-off?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) :

speechtext: So long as they were subject to call for work, they held their seniority?
Yes.

Is it clear that the terms of the well-recognized agreements between the unions and the companies are reflected in this legislation? For instance, there is the point just raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East, to which reply was made by the minister, as to what constitutes a lay-off or a severance. I imagine that is covered in the agreement between the men ana the companies. If the language of the measure preserves such contracts and agreements, then of course the situation is safe; but if the language is such that it might vary contracts or agreements, a serious question at once arises, and one which ultimately could result in differences of opinion between the workers and the companies. It seems to me we should take care that in this measure the language shall be such as to assure the preservation of the status of the different agreements.

The schedule now before the committee is practically in the language of the Washington agreement negotiated between the brotherhoods and the railways. This bill and schedule has been submitted to the eighteen brotherhoods who hold agreements with railway companies, and the wording has received their detailed examination and approval.
That is a complete answer.
I think there is no doubt *whatever that the spirit of the agreements is carried out in its language.

When the bill was before
committee on the last occasion I raised a point with regard to what I thought was unfairness to long-term employees who under the cooperative provisions of this measure might be laid off. The minister said he felt that the men with short-term service would be the ones who would likely be laid off. While there may be a certain amount of truth in the minister's statement, he must know that over a period of years there has been a continual process of laying off in the railway shops, as well as in other sections of railway activities, and the result is that to-day one will find very few working on the railways who might be described as short-term employees. Most of the employees are men
who have had service of ten or more years, and that condition has developed as a result of the continual lay-offs which have been going on over a considerable period. The figures I placed before the committee a few days ago indicate that only two-thirds the number of persons are employed on the railways as compared to the number employed seventeen years ago. The figures indicate that men with shorter terms of service have been laid off, and that only those having comparatively long terms are being retained. I suggest, therefore, that there is still a certain amount of unfairness in a clause which deals with compensation for men having service of, say, fifteen years or more.
However, as the minister has pointed out, this plan has been approved by the representatives of the great majority of railway employees, and I have no desire to ask the government to change anything which has thus been approved by the government on the one side and by the representatives of employees on the other. But if a large measure of cooperation becomes effective, as a result of legislation now in effect, this matter of compensation would no doubt be an important one confronting railway employees.
There is another matter which I believe should be brought to the attention of the minister; it is directly connected with the matter now under consideration. Hon. members realize the great financial loss suffered each year by the country through the operation of the railway companies. In the operation of the Canadian National we lose almost $1,000,000 a week, and that loss is almost exclusively chargeable to interest payments to bondholders. If we did not have that huge interest charge to meet the load would be much lighter. On two occasions the committee which deals with the Canadian National Railways has recommended that the government attempt to do something to lighten the burden of interest charges.
In one of the annual reports of the Canadian National Railways I find that in the period 1S75 to 1S83 perpetual bonds bearing five per cent interest were issued to the extent of over $20,000,000. There was another issue of perpetual bonds from 1S58 to 1876 to an amount of $13,000,000, bearing a five per cent interest rate.

Do any of them bear
a seven per cent rate?

I will come to that. In 1883, four per cent perpetual bonds were issued to the extent of $119,000,000; in 1884 four per cent bonds amounting to $1,499,000. Then
4654	COMMONS
Canadian National-C anadian Pacific Act
in 1884, four per cent perpetual guaranteed stock was issued to the extent of $60,800,000. In 1921 there was an issue of six and a half per cent guaranteed debenture bonds. Six and a half per cent is an outrageous interest charge for a government to have to pay on what might be considered a bankrupt railroad.
I do not see why something should not be done in connection with the high rates of interest paid on these perpetual bonds. The bondholders ought to bear in mind the fact that in order to meet these obligations the government is compelled to borrow money. Some hon. members will say that if we do not pay the full guaranteed rates on these securities which go back to 1858, 1875 and 1884, it would amount to repudiation. But if the yields on some of these bonds were calculated carefully it would be found that they have been paid four and five times over. In spite of what might be said, the time has come' when these rates should be cut down to three or possibly 2i per cent.
Short-term Canadian National railway bonds have been issued bearing an interest rate of only two per cent. In 1935 there was an issue of $13,400,000 at two per cent, and in 1937 there was an issue of short-term bonds at 21 per cent. If these interest rates could be brought down to the rate the government pay for money borrowed at the present time we could save considerably in excess of the $12,000,000 I suggested a few days ago on the interest charges of the Canadian National railway system.
Under this measure the railway system is to assume additional obligations. Have the government taken definite steps to do something in this particular regard? There is a strong feeling throughout the Dominion of Canada to-day that this reduction in interest charges should be made, in view of the fact that these obligations were assumed in connection with a bankrupt railroad. If I were a bondholder I think I should be ready to accept a considerable reduction in interest rates. I should feel much more secure with a bond bearing 2i per cent interest than with a perpetual bond bearing 5i or a bond bearing 64 per cent. I do not think people in any other part of the world would be prepared to be burdened with perpetual bonds going back to 1858, without having some redress against such high charges. For two successive years the railway committee suggested that something should be done, and I should like to know if the Department of Transport or the Department of Finance are doing anything about what I would almost term an intolerable situation.

My hon. friend has touched upon what constitutes the real railway problem of Canada, that is, the funded debt obligations which have been laid from time to time on the Canadian National Railways. Through the years the Canadian National Railways has never failed to pay its operating expenses and, with one or two exceptions, it has paid all charges except bond interest. The debt charges on the Canadian National Railways are abnormally high when compared with the same charges on other railways. The average debt charge on class one railways in the United States is about 16 per cent of gross revenue. The bond charges on the Canadian Pacific amount to about 17 per cent and a fraction of the gross revenue, while the interest charges on the Canadian National amount to about 27 per cent of gross revenue, which of course is entirely out of line with the charges borne by other railroads.
Anything that we can do to reduce debt charges is a partial solution of the railway problem. But there we meet the difficulty that by far the greater proportion of Canadian National Railway obligations have been guaranteed as to principal and interest by the federal government. In the early days the component railways were built with money obtained from bonds guaranteed principally by the provinces, but through the years these guarantees have been gradually taken over by the dominion government. My hon. friend has pointed out that recent borrowings have carried interest charges as low as two per cent and not higher than 3i per cent. That we are able to borrow money for the railroad at these low rates of interest, practically the same as is paid by the federal government, is due to the fact that the guarantees of the federal government on railway bonds have been honoured absolutely. If there was to be any degree of repudiation, however slight-nothing could be done in connection with a guaranteed bond without there being some slight measure of repudiation-I think the inevitable result would be that the cost of refunding, and of borrowing new money for capital improvements, would be substantially increased.
There is a point that it is well to bear in mind in connection with these perpetual bonds. While it is true that they bear a date before the beginning of the present century, with the exception of one issue of Canadian Northern bonds they are all obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway. In that connection the agreement between the government and the bondholders is dated 1919.

Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act
But interest has been paid all that time.

The bondholders have been receiving interest, but in 1919 the government took over the Grand Trunk Railway. A board of arbitrators was set up to determine the basis upon which the railway would be taken over, and it was decided that the government should continue to pay interest on the first mortgage, and certain other bonds and the preferred and common stocks were declared to be without value. As hon. members know, the government has carried out that agreement to the letter. Many times it has resisted demands, some made in this house, for the payment of the junior securities. We have refused to go beyond the award in that regard. I think the strength of our position lies in the fact that we have followed out the award in the payment of the interest on the senior securities.
This fact is very important in considering the position of these long-term and perpetual Grand Trunjc bonds. The basis of the purchase of the railway was that we would continue to pay the interest on these bonds, but would be relieved of certain other securities of the railways. As far as the government is concerned, in effect the date of these bonds is no further back than 1919. The average interest rate on all Canadian National bonds is slightly less than 4 per cent. This rate has been reduced from year to year as the bonds come due, and are refunded. The 6i per cent ifesue mentioned by my hon. friend comes due in a short time, I think within a matter of months.
Six years.

In any event the issue is comparatively small and it has not been deemed worth while to take drastic steps in respect of this particular issue. The Department of Finance has been studying the matter and conferences have been held with groups of bondholders. The Department of Finance and the board of directors of the railroad are constantly working on the various issues in an attempt to obtain adjustments more in line with present day conditions. Some progress has been made. One very important issue can be straightened out shortly, we think, by negotiation. I can assure my hon. friend that short of absolute repudiation everything is being done that can be done to meet the condition to which he has referred.

Would it be possible to call in at any time any of the perpetual five per
cent bonds?

It is not possible to call in a perpetual bond. That could be done only by negotiation or by repudiation of the perpetual feature. There is no call clause in these bonds. A perpetual bond is sometimes issued containing a clause providing for calling the bond after a number of years. A few dominion government bonds are in that position, but not these perpetual railway bonds. I should be inclined to agree that disregard of the perpetual feature would be the mildest form of repudiation that can be suggested; nevertheless it remains a type of repudiation. While some consideration has been given to the situation, no decision has been arrived at.
Would it be possible for the government to go into the market and buy these perpetual bonds-call them in in that way rather than repudiate?
Consideration has been given to this suggestion.

On the question of repudiation, and I think it is only in the nature of a suggestion, hon. members would be in a better position to discuss the matter if they had before them a picture of all the outstanding obligations of the various companies taken over under the Railway Act of 1919, under Sir Robert Borden's administration, placing this tremendous burden on the country. There were the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern and various smaller railways in some of the provinces. It was said the other day that there are over $440,000,000 of outstanding obligations in connection with the Intercolonial railway. The Intercolonial debt is not included in the Canadian National obligations.
There is practically no outstanding bonded indebtedness against the Intercolonial railway, which was paid for in cash, as constructed, out of the revenues of the dominion.

Yes, and the obligations continued to be paid. That is the reason I suggested the other day that the Intercolonial railway is in an entirely different position from that of any other railway in Canada. It was built with moneys out of the treasury of Canada, and the interest is paid. Nevertheless when Mr. Fairweather of the Canadian National Railway management brings down his statement of outstanding obligations and outstanding interest, he brings down the interest charges or deficit outstanding to-day in connection with the Intercolonial. Sometimes he makes it $4,000,000 and sometimes $5,000,000. It turns out that there are two railways in the province of Quebec which

4656	COMMONS
Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act
were never a part of the Intercolonial railway. In Nova Scotia the Halifax and Southwestern railway was taken over. It was built with subventions from federal and provincial governments, and these obligations are included in the aggregate as outstanding against the Intercolonial railway. But the Intercolonial railway stands in a different position from the Canadian National Railway system. It is a separate railway entity. The obligation in connection with its extension and operation is an obligation on all the provinces of Canada.
Under the act of 1919, which I think was a bad thing, when the Grand Trunk in the United States became part of the Canadian National railway system, the Intercolonial railway, which was built as a term of confederation, became part of the system and subject to the railway commission. At that time we were enjoying special rates, which had been in existence for forty years, to allow us to get into the central markets of Canada. Those special rates were wiped out entirely by the War Measures Act introduced by Sir Robert Borden's government, and as a result we had to place on the statute book a freight rates dct. That act is an injustice to the people of Canada. Why? Because, while special rates were given to allow the maritime provinces to get into the central markets of Canada, the Canadian Pacific Railway comes in under the general freight rates act, and with respect to every dollar that is paid out in connection with an obligation of the Intercolonial railway, which was constructed as a condition of confederation, we have to pay the piper to the Canadian Pacific as well. If the old statute had remained on the books, continuing the special rates we had enjoyed for forty-three years, practically in perpetuity, the legal position of the maritime provinces in relation to the Intercolonial railway would have been such as no other part of Canada enjoyed.
We were foolish enough in 1919 to take over practically all the railways in Canada, the Canadian Northern with its huge bond obligations, the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. My suggestion is-and I make it not in the way of criticism but for the sake of enlightenment-that the committee be given a mental picture of all the outstanding obligations in connection with the various railways now forming part of the Canadian National Railway system-the perpetual and other bonds, those bearing a high rate of interest and those bearing a lower rate of interest.
I suggest to the minister, who with his officers is giving this matter serious and continuous study, that when the tax-free war bonds were

called in, it was repudiation when we said they should no longer be tax-free but must be treated just the same as any other bond in that regard. I do not stand for repudiation in its broadest and largest sense, but I do suggest to the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Finance, and the government generally that they try to see what can be done in the way of lightening the load of interest obligations, as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North-obligations that are bearing down heavily on the people of Canada. I think it is a larger question almost than the question of amalgamation versus cooperation.
The other day, when the Minister of Transport moved the second reading of this bill, I made the statement, which I believe was correct, that Mr. Fairweather, who is the financial expert and chief of the bureau of economics of the Canadian National Railways, stated before the special committee of another chamber that the Canadian National Railways had gone as far as they could in the direction of cooperation, in the pooling of services and the elimination of. certain railways. I read the report rather hurriedly, but it seems to me that that statement was made by him, and I believe also that it was contradicted by representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The whole question is so involved that the people of this country are mystified as to the exact situation of the two systems. It is almost like being on that little boat, the Maid of the Mist, under Niagara Falls; you get on board the legislative barque of this parliament of Canada, and unless you have the real picture before you it is hard for an individual member to deal intelligently and fairly with the general situation.
As regards rates of interest on outstanding bond issues, particularly the perpetual bonds,
I cannot see that it would be in the nature of repudiation if this country should decide, after due study, that these perpetual bonds should give place, through a refunding issue, to a bond which is not perpetual. We have already refunded other outstanding obligations of the Canadian National Railways, and people have handed in their old bonds and accepted new bonds at a lower rate of interest. If that course has proved acceptable to the Canadian people who have sufficient money to own these bonds, surely if the attempt were made, not by force or duress, but through some financial compromise, we could reduce this heavy burden of interest which is weighing down our people and making such an inroad on the national income of a population of a little over eleven millions.
The problem is a serious one. The remarks I have made this morning are not in the way

Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act
of criticism but are intended to have more light thrown on the subject. I believe that at some future time the Minister of Transport, with the assistance of his technical advisers, will be able to enlighten hon. members and the people generally with a complete picture of outstanding obligations, the rates of interest they bear, and the railroads against which they are charged. We could then deal more intelligently with the question of doing away with the perpetual bond issue by the issuance of a bond guaranteed by the government carrying a lesser rate of interest. I believe that our people are patriotic enough to bear at least part of the burdens entailed by these interest charges on our great railway system, which now extends, I believe, over 35,000 miles.

In section 4, paragraph (b), line 26, occurs the word "will." "Will" is not a legal term unless it is used to designate a testament. In this case the word should be "shall."
Again:
In determining length of service of an employee ... he will be given credit.
One would think, reading the sentence as it stands, that the man gives himself credit for that service. I know I shall be told by some hon. members, as I was told the other day, that the clause is understandable. Yes, it is understandable, but so is pidgin English. I think we should aim a little higher, especially when these law's are to be interpreted by men who are learned not only in the law but also in the language. I should have thought that some other phraseology could have been used than that which appears in the section, making it clear that it was either the committee of adjustment or the board of arbitrators that was determining the length of service. Instead of the wrnrd "determining" being used as a participle they could have used the noun:
In the computation of length of service . . . he shall be given credit for performing service while so engaged. . . .
Or something to that effect. In any event the word "will" should be changed to "shall."

This language has been
threshed over a good many times. It is the language of the Washington agreement.
I do not care whose language it is.

I should be very pleased to change "will" to "shall" except that, as my hon. friend knows, this bill has already passed the senate, and I should not like to send it back there-they might change their minds about it.
Just give the senate warning that they must watch their English.

Paragraph agreed to.
Paragraph (c) agreed to.
On paragraph (d).

This subsection has to do not only with the question of compensation but with the matter of a person being asked to return to work who is receiving compensation as the result of the measure we are now discussing. A good many employees are receiving fairly low wages, and according to this measure they will be entitled, in case they are laid off as a result of any cooperative effort, to sixty per cent of the amount of their salary or wages as compensation. A man whose wages have averaged about $70 a month-and that is about the compensation of a great many employees- will be entitled to sixty per cent of $70, or $42 a month. A man cannot live with any degree of decency on so small a sum, and I have been wondering whether it would not have been wiser and better that persons who receive so low a rate of compensation should be allowed to augment it if they have the opportunity of doing so, without infringing upon the conditions of the measure we are now considering.
They are quite at liberty to augment their earnings in any way they like, provided that that way is not service for a railway.

Then do I understand that an employee of the railway who is receiving compensation as a result of cooperative efforts, and whose compensation amounts, let us say, to the figure of $42, can go out and obtain other employment and receive his compensation over the period of two or three or five years, as the case may be?
He can start other employment the day he is laid off, if he likes to do so. He still gets his separation allowance from the railway.
He can take a full-time position anywhere else the moment he is removed from the service?
Oh, yes.
And still be entitled to compensation?

Yes. He is still on call for the railway, but provided he is not called he can work at any employment he likes; just as a railway shopman laid off to-day can accept other employment without disturbing his rights with his railway. This compensa-
4658	.	COMMONS
Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act
tion has relation entirely to employment by the railways. A man can engage in any other activity he likes, provided he is always on call for the railway. He must report back when he is called.
Is there anything in this bill that distinctly corroborates the minister's statement as to the facts of the matter?
This agreement simply states what the employee must do in relation to the railways. It places no restrictions upon his activities in other lines.

It applies only to men
laid off in consequence of cooperation between the railways, but not to lines that may be torn up by one railway which may consider such lines no longer necessary?

That is correct. It applies
only to lay-offs resulting from an agreement entered into under the terms of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act.
Is this retroactive?
No.

It does not apply to men
laid off in the last few years?

No. It distinctly applies to
employees now or hereafter to be employed by the railways.

Is this legislation intended to
be perpetual, or is it merely to fill in a gap? Is it likely to be repealed by the present government?
I do not think my'hon. friend would ask me to bind future parliaments, but so long as I am Minister of Transport it will not be repealed.
Would paragraph (e) cover the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway? Was the question considered of widening the scope of the provision in order to cover temporary employment with that railway?

The Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway operates under provincial charter, and the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act applies only to the two railways therein named. This would not affect agreements with the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway.

On section 8, paragraph (a).

There is a queer twist in the phraseology here. The important words in the paragraph are in line 22 "to be named." Those are the dominant words. Three arbitrators are to be named, one by the representatives of the interested employees and one by the representatives of the Canadian National company and the Canadian Pacific company and the third by the two so named, "or, in case the two arbitrators so named fail to agree on the selection of the third arbitrator, the Minister of Labour shall make such selection." Why not say "or by the minister?" If you wish to use the phraseology used here you should say "but" instead of "or": "but if the two so named cannot agree the minister shall make the selection." It must not be forgotten that the dominant words are "to be named." Otherwise the sentence is involved and it is difficult to understand. It may be said that sending it back to the senate would entail some trouble, but they are not averse to correcting our language, and quite properly so.

This is the language of the Washington agreement and when we pass this schedule we shall have a uniform law applying to all north America so far as this particular act is concerned. Such uniformity is desirable and perhaps overrides any slight ambiguity my hon. friend may detect in the paragraph. No one will question the procedure intended under the bill. I agree that the wording may be a trifle cumbersome, but that hardly justifies our departing from the language of the Washington agreement.
I am not moving an amendment, nor am I asking the minister to have one moved, but I should like to know who drafted the famous Washington agreement.

I suppose it was the result of the combined legal talents of the railways and the brotherhoods.

The Canadian railways and brotherhoods?

No. The Canadian railways are represented through the Grand Trunk Western, which is a United States line, but the responsibility rests with the United States railways and the brotherhoods, which are international.

Are the railway brotherhoods satisfied to have only one representative?
I notice that in cases of disputes they will have one and the railways one each, and these two will appoint a fourth.
There is only one representative for the two railways.

Does the Washington
agreement cover agreements between the unions and the men?

The Washington agreement
covers only compensation in the event of consolidations in the United States. One party is the railways and the other the employees represented through their brotherhoods.
It does not cover any agreements between the head office of the brotherhood and the men directly?
No.
When does this agreement come into effect?
As soon as royal assent is given, which we hope will be in a very few days.
Does this bill cover employees -who are not members of any of the railway men's organizations? Does it apply to such employees who may lose their positions in consequence of cooperation?

It covers every employee of the railways. Most railway employees are represented by a union; I know of no class }f employee who is not. The only significance of the union is that in connection with the board of arbitration which is set up under the act it is provided that the union holding the agreement covering that class of employee will be the instrument through which one member of the arbitration board is appointed. That is the only way the unions come into it, but every employee is covered.
Is there not some sort of board of adjustment on which the employees and employers are represented, to look after any grievances that may arise under this measure?
Certainly.
Who will appoint the members of that board?

Can my hon. friend mention any class of railway employees not represented by unions? I suppose the extra gang labour would not be, but that would not come under the agreement because it is only temporary labour with no seniority rights involved. Aside from that I know of no class of employees not represented by some branch of a union holding an agreement with the railways.
I had more in mind the office employees.
They are all unionized, so far as I know.

I understand that the
standard labour organizations have approved this bill, but that it has not been approved by the Canadian brotherhood organizations. In case there is a dispute in which the Canadian brotherhoods are involved, how are the arbitrators selected?

Where the Canadian brotherhoods hold the agreement covering that class of labour, the Canadian union would select the representative. speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, May 25, consideration in committee of Bill No. 130, to provide for the constitution of a salt fish board-Mr. Michaud-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 5-Duties of board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
When we were discussing this section the other day the committee rose at six o'clock and I had no opportunity to make the remarks I desired to make. However, as a result of the statement on that occasion by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), who L regret is not in his place to-day, one thing stands out sc
Salt Fish Board

clearly that it cannot be allowed to pass without being brought to the attention of the government. Subsection (a) of this section states:
The board shall
(a) investigate and report to the minister upon the marketing of salt fish in the export trade and explore all possibilities of opening up new marketing outlets;
I am afraid I must agree with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) when he says we are taking away the functions of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Already there has been some invasion by the Department of Agriculture, and now we find the Department of Fisheries taking over some of the work which in my opinion belongs to the Department of Trade and Commerce. It becomes quite clear that the Minister of Trade and Commerce now will have only a motion picture bureau to look after, since all the other functions of his department are to be taken over by other branches of the government. In the course of his remarks the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
Our chief competitors are Newfoundland, Norway and Iceland. Newfoundland is perhaps as strong a competitor as we have. The people of Newfoundland are almost confined to the production of one commodity, namely fish-
I think that should be underlined, because it is very important.
The people of Newfoundland are almost confined to the production of one commodity, namely fish

Further on the minister said:
Most of our market is in western Cuba, although in that market Newfoundland is now becoming a strong competitor.
And further on:
Then, our market in the British West Indies is not as good as it was. Newfoundland has become a keen competitor.
In other words, the Minister of Trade and Commerce advanced the argument that because Newfoundland has become a strong competitor of Canada it has become necessary to subsidize the fishing industry of Nova Scotia. At this point I want to make it quite clear that I heartily endorse any proposal to help the fishermen of that province-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Of the maritimes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Yes, but I wonder if this is the best method we can adopt to help our fishermen. After all, what does this mean? Here we have an appropriation of about $800,000 that we propose to spend in order to help out the salt fish industry of the maritime provinces. In the first place we are seeking to destroy the markets of a country with which we are on very friendly terms.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has made it quite clear that the people of Newfoundland live chiefly through the production of fish. So far as I know we have nothing at all against the people of that country; we have very friendly relations with them and we would like to help them, but the way we are going to help them is lay taking away their only means of livelihood. We say we must destroy their markets in order to gain them for ourselves, and to do that we are going to subsidize our fishing industry.
In the second place, Mr. Chairman, by a subsidy of this nature we are lowering the cost of Canadian fish not to Canadian consumers but to consumers in Cuba. ' We say we cannot compete with Newfoundland because their prices are lower than ours, so we are going to subsidize our industry. In other words we are simply lowering the price of Canadian fish to the consumer of western Cuba. It seems to me we should be able to go about this business in a much better way than that. Instead of reducing the cost of our fish to the inhabitants of western Cuba I would prefer to reduce the cost of our fish to the inhabitants of western Canada or of western Ontario. If we intend to spend $800,000 it does not make much difference to us whether we spend it in one way or another, but I believe we should spend it to the best advantage of Canada as a whole. Therefore I suggest to the minister that it should be possible to take this $800,000 and give it as a discount to the Canadian dealer instead of to the Canadian exporter. As a result the price of fish to the Canadian consumer would be lowered. I know it is argued that the question of transportation enters into the fresh fish industry, but this measure deals with salt fish only, so the transportation question does not enter at all. We can ship our fish from the maritimes to western Canada or western Ontario, or as far as we like as a matter of fact, and keep it in very good condition. I would ask the minister to tell me whether he does not think this suggestion is entirely reasonable. Instead of giving a subsidy to make Canadian fish cheaper for western Cubans, why not give a subsidy to make Canadian fish cheaper for Canadians? In so far as giving help to the industry is concerned it will amount to the same thing. The fishermen do not care where the sales are made, so long as they are made. If the minister intends to bonus the industry, then why not bonus it on sales made in Canada instead of those made in western Cuba? If that were done,, what would 'be the result? We would not be taking anything away from Newfoundland. They need their markets,

Salt Fish Board
because as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated repeatedly, that is their only means of earning a livelihood.
How do we propose to help ourselves? It is suggested we help ourselves by taking from Newfoundland their only means of livelihood. I suggest that instead of bonusing the exporters of fish the minister should use the $800,000 to give a discount to dealers in Canada, and thus help the industry and at the same time help the Canadian consumer, and not the consumer of western Cuba. I hope the minister will realize I make these observations in a spirit of helpfulness. I am not attempting to criticize the desire to help the fishermen of the maritime provinces. I want them to have prosperity, the same as other people in Canada. But I do suggest our first consideration should be for the Canadian consumer rather than the consumer of western Cuba. I believe my argument is worthy of careful consideration. I might add-and perhaps at the same time destroy the argument I have been making-that that is one of the principles for which hon. members in this group stand.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
That would not be
unusual.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: What about wheat?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: We are not dealing with wheat just now; we are dealing with salt fish. But wheat is a commodity of which we have an abundance in western Canada, whereas we do not get as much fish as we could use.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The principle is the same.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I have to pay about thirty-five cents a pound for fish in western Canada, and it is therefore evident that many of our consumers cannot get it. This piece of legislation is an example of the folly of attempting to compete with a friendly nation to benefit ourselves and at the same time destroy their trade, when we might improve our trade more easily and to greater advantage by extending sales within our own country. I suggest that the conditions with respect to wheat would not be the same because of the vast amount of wheat that is exported. But in this instance we are dealing with an expenditure of only $800,000, and we have before us a striking example of what could be done by using that money in Canada to our own advantage. I hope the minister will consider my suggestion carefully. There may be technical flaws in my argument, but he will have to work out the technical details in connection with subsidizing exports. In any event, I do not think
technical details would destroy the truth of the argument I have been making.
The Minister of Fisheries, in collaboration with his colleagues in the government, has all kinds of experts available to work out technical details. They are not for me to worry about. I am concerned only with the idea of giving the preference to the Canadian consumer rather than the consumer of western Cuba, and I suggest my representations should be given serious consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is selfish, not salt fish.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I might add it looks like a fishy way of doing it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
In view of the evident concern of the hon. member for Peace River, may I assure him there is no intention to invade the prerogatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce, nor is it felt by the minister at the head of that department that his prerogatives are being invaded by the Department of Fisheries. There is no danger that the government of the country will be upset by the invasion by the Department of Fisheries of the prerogatives and duties of other departments. It is not our intention to assume duties, in connection with finding markets for Canadian products, which heretofore have been discharged by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
As the hon. member is no doubt aware, in these days the marketing* of processed fish, due to exacting taste and requirements of consumers abroad, has become very difficult, and there is the further difficulty experienced by the fishermen of adapting themselves to the production of that type of product demanded by the consumer. In its investigation of the marketing of salt fish the object of the Department of Fisheries is, first, to investigate the needs of people who in the past have bought our fish, but have since made evident their preference for the product of competing countries. In some instances they claim our goods are not as well prepared and not put up in as good quality as those of other countries. It is our intention to have the board find out what the consumers want, and we feel that to acquire that information we must have the services of experts in the fishing business. That is why we ask wide powers for the board. Then, in the second place, we want to investigate methods of preparing fish which have been adopted by our competitors, and place that information within the immediate reach of the producers and processors of salt fish. That is a further duty to which we feel the board should apply itself.
Salt Fish Board

If the hon. member has been anywhere on the Atlantic coast where people live through what they gain from the fisheries he must know that the fishermen go to sea in the morning and come back in the evening, and because of their location and environment, and their limited educational facilities, they have difficulty in following the methods adopted in foreign markets where they must meet competition. The department is looking into that matter on their behalf, and we are transferring to the members of the board duties which in the past have been assumed by officials in the department. As hon. members must realize, the board will be nothing more or less than a branch of the Department of Fisheries. It will be under the control of the department and particular duties will be assigned to it.
On that score the hon. member need not fear any invasion of the prerogatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We will confine ourselves to the business of finding better markets for the producers of salt fish, ascertaining whaf consumers in foreign countries want, and how we can produce those goods at a cost low enough to enable us to compete with the products of other countries.
The hon. member has said that we are going to affect the rights of the Newfoundland fishermen. It must not be forgotten that markets now being enjoyed by our competition from Newfoundland were at one time the markets enjoyed by Canadian fishermen. The fishermen of Newfoundland have been successful in invading what might be described as our markets because they have adopted certain measures which heretofore our fishermen have not enjoyed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Through subsidies.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The government of Great Britain has undertaken the administration of Newfoundland and is providing large sums of money for the welfare of those people. I understand that the amount voted this year comes close to $5,000,000, which will be employed for the relief of Newfoundland. They are able to give us serious competition in our markets. Should we lie down and let them invade our markets without adopting similar methods to enable our fishermen to compete? I feel, and those connected with the fishing industry feel, that we should adopt some measures to enable our fishermen to meet their most serious competition.
My hon. friend has made the statement that this subsidy will reduce the cost of fish to the consumers in Cuba, which country my hon. friend has taken to exemplify his argument. There are two sections of Cuba

to be considered, the east and the west. The people in the warmer climates eat more fish than the Canadian people do. They have to have it, they cannot produce it, and that is why we strive so hard to capture and maintain these markets. The people in Havana for many years have refused to use our fish in large quantities because they claim it is not up to the standard they require; they say they will not take our fish until it is prepared to their particular requirements. On the other hand, the people of Santiago like our fish and the manner in which it is prepared.
In recent years the fishermen of Newfoundland, Norway and Iceland have been granted subsidies which have enabled them to supply-fish of a high grade at a very low price, so much so that our producers cannot meet the competition and make a profit. We feel that in order to induce people to use our fish we should meet the prices of our competitors. We do not want to reduce the market price, but we do want to enable our fishermen to produce fish of the required standard and quality and at the same time make a living. This must be done if we are to sell any' fish on these markets. My hon. friend suggests that we should direct our activities toward the bonusing of salt fish for Canadian consumption. We must not overlook the fact that the Canadian people do not eat the same amount of fish as do the people in the southern countries, and for that reason our market is limited. Then if we go too far west, we meet the reproaches of the fishermen on the Pacific coast who produce more than half the total production in Canada. They claim they must have the markets of the western provinces. Then the fishermen on the great lakes want to preserve their market in the central provinces. To subsidize the fishermen in eastern Canada in order to enable them to compete with the fishermen of central Canada and the Pacific coast would not be reasonable or fair.
My hon. friend must know that during last winter and the winter before, considerable quantities of salt fish were sent to the western provinces for relief purposes. There was an immediate reaction from the fish dealers in the western provinces who claimed that we were invading their markets. We have to be careful in whatever policy we adopt in the marketing of Canadian products. We must not favour one group at the expense of another. The benefits of this legislation are applied only to the export of salt fish because that is where we have our most serious competition. To vote money to permit the fishermen in one part of Canada to compete with the fishermen in another part would be illogical and unfair. I suggest that we should

Salt Fish Board
do our 'best under difficult circumstances to help this class of people who unfortunately are not in a position to help themselves. I admit that the legislation is not perfect. It is only an experiment and many defects may be found in it. But it is a step forward; it is the first attempt made to help these people. If all cooperate I think we shall succeed in bringing about a measure of relief to a class of people who certainly deserve it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The minister said that he intended to use fishermen from the eastern coast who know something about fishing in order to discover new methods of packing and preparation. I do not think that meets the contention I was making, that this is largely an invasion of the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce. There is no reason why that department should not have its experts, fishermen if you like, go into the matter of devising new methods of packing and preparing. As a matter of fact, I believe the Department of Trade and Commerce has representatives abroad who are supposed to feel the pulse of foreign markets in order to keep home industry advised.
So far as the bill itself is concerned, it is not a question of whether it is a good thing to bonus producers. That is beside the point; it is a question which has been dealt with already. We have decided to do it, and all I am asking is that it should be done to the advantage of the Canadian consumer instead of to the advantage of the consumer in Cuba. The minister has said that the western Cuban likes our fish. I do not doubt that at all. But the western Canadian also likes eastern Canadian salt fish and would be glad to get it. If I had not suggested an alternative market to that of Cuba, then my argument could not stand. But there is no doubt that western Ontario and the western provinces could absorb that small amount of bonus which we intend to give to assist the people on the eastern coast.
The minister said that we are assisting various classes in Canada by giving bonuses- the great lakes fishermen, the fishermen on the western coast and others-but he did not refer to the injury this might do to the fishermen of Newfoundland, whose only livelihood is fishing. The minister said over and over again that all that Newfoundland had to depend on was the fisheries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I do not feel that it is within the scope of my duties to look after Newfoundland.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Quite so; but the minister should not destroy the livelihood of the people of a country with which we have
friendly relations. However, I thought I would make my suggestion to the minister because this appeared to be an ideal opportunity to put it into practice with reference to this-Canadian industry. It is not necessary to refer to other branches of Canadian industry because fishing is the only one we are considering at the moment. Generally speaking, this is not a vast sum of money; we have spent larger amounts, but it deals with one particular industry and one type of product, a product for which we cannot find a market within Canada. Every factor is present in this industry for trying out this new method of economics. The minister says that this measure is simply an experiment, that it is not perfect. Of course, no legislation dealing with something of which we have had no previous experience can be regarded as other than experimental, an attempt to move forward; and I do say that this affords a splendid opportunity to take a forward step, instead of relying, as we always have done in the past, on finding foreign markets. I hope that the minister will consider the suggestion I have made because I feel it is worthy of consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The hon. member for Peace River suggests that we sell fish in the Canadian market and give the Canadian consumer the benefit. Let me compare the Canadian market to the foreign market to show how the fishermen would benefit from such a policy as he suggests. In 1937 we produced 211,432 hundredweight of dried cod, and we exported 205.992 hundredweight, leaving 5.540 hundredweight for Canadian consumption. Suppose-you made it $5 a hundredweight. The fishermen of the maritime provinces, about 20,000 in number, would benefit to the extent of about $5,000, or about 25 cents apiece in a year. That w-ould follow from the policy suggested by the hon. member for Peace River.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: This bill is not confined to-dried codfish.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is a big item.

speechtext:
This bill is for the purpose
of assisting in the development of an export market. There are two classes of people engaged in this industry in the maritimes, the fisherman and the exporter. The fisherman in Nova Scotia to-day, unless he is a bank fisherman, with vessels and crews to catch fish, is both a fisherman and an exporter, and one of the safeguards that we should place around this bill is this. We are practically voting $800,000 to assist the exporter to sell his fish in foreign markets, in Cuba, the West Indies, Italy and whatever other markets are
Salt Fish Board

available. In my judgment-I may be wrong, and perhaps the Minister of Fisheries may be able to change my view-no person who is going to benefit from the receipt of any part of this 8800,000 should be a member of the board. I think that should be made clear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is clear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The minister says that
that is clear, but I cannot see it. It should be an independent board. The major power should remain and be inherent in the Department of Fisheries. The board should not be very much more than an advisory board. If you are going to have exporters make regulations as to the ordinary marketing of fish and the manner in which it shall be put up-because they are the people who are going to do it, and they are the people who are going to receive this $800,000-it will not be an independent board. We should have an independent board that will be fair to the fisherman, fair to the exporter and at the same time help to rehabilitate the salt fish industry and the various classes of fish which will be exported under the provisions of this bill. The exporter should have no fiduciary relations whatever with the board, no more than a member of parliament can be in receipt of anything beyond what the statute permits him to receive, his sessional indemnity and, if he is a minister of the [DOT]crown, his pay as such. The moment you go beyond that you make a monopoly of it, because the exporter has control of the 8800,000, and unlike another bill before us this morning, this bill does not say "may" but "shall," and "shall" means "must." It is [DOT]a monopoly. I think it is a proper time to see that our exporters of fish are treated fairly and that the fisherman is also given a [DOT]chance as to price. The board should be absolutely independent to protect the interests of the fisherman who has fish to sell to the exporter, and we should not permit the exporter to make conditions such as will give him a monopoly. While he is making these regulations he will be putting the money in his own pocket. I do not mean that in an unfair way, but if this measure is to be a success, the members of the board should not, beyond what they receive for their services, participate in the export of fish to any market because they have the inside track. They are like the horse; I do not know much about horse racing, but they seem to have the pull. I make that suggestion to the minister, and if the bill in that respect is not clear as it stands, it should be made clear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
It would be better for
them not only to have the pull but to win the prize.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
My hon. friend comes from
a province where they always have the pull and win the prize as well.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Powers of board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I should like before this passes to make one more comment on the phraseology of the intent of the bill. The section reads: "give assistance to exporters." When I find in spite of what has been said by the minister, a member such as the member for Kent (Mr. Robichaud) expressing dubiety as to the meaning, and a member with the experience and ability in interpreting the law of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) saying plainly that he believes the section means "aid the exporters," I think I am justified in falling back on common sense and the dictionary meaning and regarding "exporter" as meaning one who exports.
If they hold that point of view, then it would appear that the whole bill is framed around giving benefits to the exporters.
I should like to point out by way of comparison what is done in another country. The whole purport of this bill, we are told . by hon. members from the maritimes-and I believe they are sincere in saying so-is to give aid to the working fisherman. Well then, by all that is wonderful, why not say so? Why not put it in language that cannot be misunderstood? It is the working fisherman who is up against it, who is on the edge of relief or starvation, and we propose to help him. What more definite way could be followed than to say it in language which any of us could understand? Here is an illustration of what a neighbouring country has done.
I hold in my hand an article from the current number of the Financial Post describing how the Newfoundland government subsidizes the salt cod fish industry. It reads in part as follows:
Newfoundland fishermen are being guaranteed a minimum price for their catch of cod fish during 1938.
Observe the words "fishermen," "guaranteed" and "price."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: How is that done?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
That is a matter of detail.
I am dealing with what they have done. The Newfoundland government is really a commission government under the British government. The article goes on to say that the commission government of Newfound-

Salt Fish Board
land has established minimum prices to be paid by exporters to fishermen. Could language be more plain or more welcome to the working fishermen? They not only are going to fix but they have fixed the price to be paid by exporters to the fishermen. Further on it says:
Minimum prices to be paid to fishermen at designated export points are given below.
And then those prices and points are given. The man who is out on the coast, away out of touch with anything, knows, if he goes out and gets a certain quantity of fish, exactly what he can get for them. Is not that satisfactory to him, and ought it not to be to us? Then the article says:
Exporter is free to sell at the best price he can get.
There is no trouble such as we had the other day trying to dope out how the benefits would filter down or drip down from the exporter, backwards-a very difficult way-to the fishermen. Here it begins with the fishermen, and it says, "You will get" presumably "a reasonable price." The prices fixed appear to be reasonable. The fisherman knows exactly what he is going to get. The government takes the responsibility and pays the loss to the exporter after taking into consideration what labour charges have been put on. It seems to me that that is exactly what we are trying to do in this bill. If that is the case, why mix it up by vague or doubtful interpretations of what an exporter is? The Newfoundland government know what they are doing. They have done it before; they did it in September, and they say that it worked satisfactorily. Why not follow this precedent?
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare says, how will they do it? I suppose they will pass an order in council fixing the price.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: But how do they pay the money?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: If I am correctly informed, payment under the Newfoundland scheme is made by the government to the exporter, on condition that the exporter pays these prices to fishermen. Do I make myself clear?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: No. It is a decree, as to price.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is exactly what can be done under this act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: It is compulsory.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: If you had the regulations of the Newfoundland government before you, von would doubtless find that the Newfoundland government or the commission is authorized to pay the exporters, out of the money supplied by the British government, the difference between what they are told to pay the fishermen and what they get in the foreign market.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: No, that is not it. I have had an opportunity of looking it up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I have been told that that is it. I shall be glad to be informed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: This article says that the government pays the exporters the loss, but they start in with the fixed price to the fishermen; and you cannot show me within the confines of this bill where the fishermen are guaranteed anything at all.

speechtext: They may be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Yes, they may be, but the exporter, when it comes to him passing back the money, will find all kinds of reasons why he cannot afford to pay. But here it begins at the basic place. The fisherman has to get the fixed price; he knows about it. Is that the case under this bill?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The bill authorizes the same thing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Then why not say so?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The government absorbs
the loss plus a profit to the exporter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I do not feel that I should discuss this bill at any length. It does apply, of course, to the fishing districts of Quebec. It should be so arranged by appointing an advisory committee for the fishing districts of Quebec, or by appointing a member on this central board, that the interests of the Quebec fishermen are looked after to just the same extent and as advantageously as the fishermen of Nova Scotia. I am astonished that not a single member from Quebec has, apparently, taken the trouble to study this bill or to suggest to the house in what way it might be improved so as to serve the Quebec fishing interests. I do not know sufficient about the fishing interests of Quebec to discuss in detail the application of the scheme to their interests, but I am convinced after due consideration, and after having listened to the information supplied by the ministers and by hon. members who participated in the discussion, that this bill offers no definite advantage to the shore fishermen of Nova Scotia.

IMr. Michaud.)
thing for the boat fisherman, who catches the fish, though I conceive that it may be to the advantage of the fisherman who has a share in a fishing vessel which is engaged in bank fishing, and I am glad that he may-get some advantage. The Newfoundland government in its discretion has prescribed by decree the minimum prices that shall be paid the fishermen. That is the basis of the Newfoundland law at the present time. The fisherman of Newfoundland is assured of a minimum price no matter what happens to the fish afterwards, and that fixed price is of very great advantage to him. It is true that the exporter is also taken care of, because the exporter under the law of Newfoundland is entitled to receive the minimum price which is paid to the fisherman plus so many cents a quintal for labour in gathering the fish at the outport for export; so much at St. Johns and another price at other outports. He is also allowed certain other overhead charges. For instance, the price paid the fishermen in St. Johns will be $4.25 a quintal plus overhead labour and a special allowance amounting to 75 cents or a total of $5.00, and the-difference will be payable by the government; that is to say, the losses of exporters who-have paid the minimum prices, established bylaw, plus the overhead charges for labour and other items allowed by law are paid by the-government. In other words, the exporter will receive whatever price he can obtain in the foreign market, but such losses as the exporter-may incur are an additional charge upon the government funds and will be paid by the-government.

speechtext: And the minister agrees as to the difficulty.
