Then if the price obtained is not sufficient to cover the price paid the fisherman, plus fixed allowances, the government would pay to the exporter the difference, so that he would not lose on the transaction. That is the Newfoundland scheme, and it is workable. I admit the scheme before the committee is workable so far as bank fishermen are concerned, but it seems to me difficult of application in respect of those hundreds of individuals along the coast of Nova Scotia who go out in the morning, fish during the day and return at sundown with their catch, a part of which they may be able to sell to purchasers of fresh fish for domestic or export trade, and another part of which, if not sold fresh, must be dried or pickled. It is that man whose interests chiefly concern me, because in years gone by, and in recent years, travelling around that coast, I have seen his misery.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I assure the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that much consideration and thought has been given to the Newfoundland legislation, and that the department has come to the conclusion that the legislation we now propose would be easier land cheaper of administration than the method adopted in Newfoundland. We must not overlook the fact that there are certain constitutional limitations to whatever action we may take.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: What are they?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: They are these: First of all, we cannot enact compulsory legislation which could apply to fish marketed or prepared for market in Quebec, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and the Magdalen Islands.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I am not so sure about that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
It is possible that my hon. friend may not be sure about it, and I should have liked to share his doubts or even his conviction to the contrary. Unfortunately I had to come to the conclusion that there were limitations, and that we could not overstep those limitations without subjecting ourselves to the risk of nullification of our good intentions.
The hon. member will notice that the Newfoundland legislation is compulsory, and is composed of three factors: First, the fisherman must make himself a member of the fishing society or cooperative organization, and take out a licence to fish. Second, the board has complete power to prevent anyone who does not comply with regulations from exporting fish, and third, it has the further power to exact penalties for violation of the provisions. The measure is compulsory, and those who wish to derive any benefit from the Newfoundland legislation are compelled to come under the jurisdiction of the board and pay a set price to the fishermen. Then only are they entitled to compensation for whatever losses they may have in the export or sale of goods on which they have paid a compulsory price to the fishermen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Is it not true that under this bill the exporter of fish-I am referring to the man who actually exports-will have to do certain things and conform to certain regulations similar to the regulations in Newfoundland in order to share in the bonus or assistance provided by this bill?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Yes, but it is the intention of the bill to grant the benefits only to those exporters who comply with the regulations. However, the bill is not compulsory.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I do not think it would prove to be a hardship to make the exporters who' will come under this bill-again I am referring to the real exporters-take out a nominal licence so that their names and addresses would be known. The licence to export issued in Newfoundland is nominal in character. As I understand it, while a man is not prevented from exporting fish without a licence, if he wishes to take advantage of the bonus or the assistance given by the government he must take out the nominal licence and comply with the regulations imposed upon all licencees.

Salt Fish Board

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will find that under the Newfoundland legislation no one can export salt or dried fish unless he is licensed. A man is penalized for exporting without having first taken out a licence. In this country there are other restrictions, such as those imposed by geography. For example, the assistance to be rendered under this bill may not necessarily be the same in the case of a fisherman on the Labrador coast or the Magdalen islands as it would in the case of the Lunenburg fishermen. The intention of the short amendment I have suggested is to make this clearer and enable the board to deal with the fishermen in each section in a manner that will be most suitable to the local circumstances.
It has been said that in some sections it would be of more benefit to the fishermen if advances in kind were made instead of a bonus being paid on the quantity of fish exported during or at the end of the season. An advance of salt at the beginning of the season has been suggested in order to enable the fishermen to prepare and cure their fish. This would be the most practical method of helping the fishermen along the north shore of the St. Lawrence and on the Gaspe coast. With the twenty-five per cent limitation in mind we want to empower the board to make a rough estimate of the market value of the fish in order that advances may be made at or from the beginning of the season either in the form of money or in materials such as salt. This would provide assistance for the fishermen who otherwise would not be able to put up any salt fish during the season.
It was felt by the department and others connected with the fisheries that a single method of assistance could not be made applicable to all fishermen. As I said before, the fishermen on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, on the Gaspe coast and along the Labrador coast must be dealt with differently. The fishermen on the Magdalen islands must also be dealt with in a different manner. The fishermen on the Magdalen islands and along the north shore of New Brunswick have claimed that the best method of assisting them would be for the board to absorb the cost of transportation from the point of production to Halifax, from which port exportations of fish to the south are usually made. This is why section 6 has been drafted in its present form.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
After all, this is the main section of the bill and. as I read it I am impressed with the thought that the government and the minister, in an effort to assist the fishing industry of the maritimes, concluded that if there could be an expansion in
exports the benefits of such expansion would' work back to the fishermen. In a very~ general way, that is a sound deduction to-make. Therefore, in framing the bill they decided that the best plan was to bonus the-exporter, and, subject to these minor explanations which have been made but which are not in the bill, it is hoped that the benefits-which will accrue to the exporter will be equitably distributed back to the producer.. In my opinion there is a definite objection to that theoretical approach to the problem. The element of human nature enters into the-question. While I would not for one moment want to reflect upon a class of persons such as-exporters, with our knowledge of human nature we must realize that a bonus cannot be paid to an ultimate exporter with the assurance that a reasonable and equitable proportion will voluntarily be translated back to an inarticulate and unorganized producer. To* my mind that is the weakness in the philosophy of this legislation.
Let me approach it from another point of view. Undoubtedly there is in the minds of all of us a desire to help a most needy person,, namely, the primary producer. He is the-person whom we want to benefit. Speaking for myself, I should never be inclined to support legislation for the purpose of bonusing some business concern. My theory is that a business concern is quite able to look after itself. But when we come to deal with the worker who is unable under present-day-economic conditions to protect himself, then I think parliament is justified in entering the-picture. If we examine this section I think we will find that in spite of the fact that the term "exporter" has been broadened-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: In my opinion it has not-been broadened at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I was trying t-o give the government a little credit, but I shall retract that statement. In spite of the fact that the term "exporter" as defined in the bill is in my opinion wholly inadequate to meet the situation, what we are doing in effect is benefiting exporters. We have the pious hope that under paragraph Ob) of section 6 regulations of some sort will be designed which will carry that 'benefit back to the other parties" to the transaction, the producer, the drier,, the salter and what not. But it is only a-pious hope. If you will read paragraph (bl you will find there is nothing statutory to-say that it shall be done. We simply say that the board may pass regulations and from time to time vary the terms and conditions.. Vary what terms and conditions? We do not state any terms and conditions. It is another illustration of the loose draftsmanship that
[DOT]4670
Salt Fish Board

characterizes modern legislation passing through this house. The old theory of legislation was that every statute must set *out clearly the powers and rights and privileges conferred-the powers to do and the rights to enjoy. Then the administrators of the statute would be empowered to make regulations " not inconsistent with the terms of the act "-that was the expression commonly used. But you do not say that here. The minister, very generously and in a kindly spirit, expressed the hope that when this board was formed certain benefits would find their way back to the producer. He says he intends that they should. But I must remind him that what is in his mind and in his heart is not law. It has no statutory power. It is not an instruction to do. There is nothing [DOT]obligatory upon the board to do it. It is, as the legislation is drafted, merely permissible. There is nothing more or less than a pious hope that it will be done.
There is another objection to the manner in which this bill is drafted. No board operating under this statute, I care not how fine the men are or how good-hearted or how wise they may be, can possibly be immune from prejudices of one kind and another which [DOT]enter into the administration of law. One of the things which administrators are up against *every day, and the minister knows it, is the importunity of friends and the pressure of interests of various kinds; and his protection invariably is, "Well, I am very sorry I cannot do it, because it is contrary to the law." Now this board, which is to have more or less of a free hand, will be subjected to all the pressure and influences to which I have just referred. So I think this clause ought to be redrafted in order to make it clear, in the first place, that the benefits to be derived from the grant of $800,000 are to accrue by law to the exporter, if you like, but also-and this should be explicitly stated in the section-to the producer and the intermediate processor.
In the second place we should set out in *statutory form in paragraph (b) the groundwork for the regulations. I know the argument -I have heard it too long not to know it- that you cannot put into a statute phraseology that will be sufficiently elastic. But that is not so. You can fix the principles of the -legislation, then you can give wide powers, prescribing what shall be done, when it shall be done, and how it shall be done, so long as it is not inconsistent with the powers and rights conferred.
I am sorry to differ from the minister, but frankly I do not believe this measure will achieve what be has in his mind, as expressed by himself in kindly and courteous terms both to-day and on a previous occasion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The solicitude and concern of the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) for the welfare of the individual fisherman is to be commended, but I may tell him that his is no greater than that of members of this government. He claims that the act is drafted, if not with the intention, at least with the effect of benefiting the exporter. That may be true in a sense, but upon the meaning of "exporter" apparently we do not agree. The act is drawn and presented for the approval of the house for the purpose of benefiting a class of fishermen who will direct part of their catch of fish to the salt fish branch of the industry and for export. This must not be overlooked. In order to attain that object we have defined the person who shall be entitled to benefit. We designate him as an "exporter," but not giving to the word "exporter" its general meaning. We have stated in section 2, paragraph (d), that "exporter" means:
... a person or cooperative group of fishermen owning fish which is afterwards exported in a salted state-
In my opinion there is no possible escape for the board from helping the person who processes fish for export.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The definition includes three distinct classes of persons as exporters, but there are no provisions for the distribution of the bonus or benefits among these three different classes of people.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I agree. In order to
enable the board to pass along the benefits of the act to any one of the three classes which we contemplate will benefit, we have enacted in section 6 that:
The board may-
(a)	give assistance to exporters-
That is, to any class of persons who come under the definition of "exporters":
-in such form and manner and to such extent as may from time to time be determined by the board and approved by the government in council, provided that the assistance given to any exporter during any marketing season shall not exceed in value twenty-five per centum of the value as estimated or found by the board at the point and time of export of the fish in respect of which such assistance is given.
(b)	with the approval of the governor in council establish by regulation and from time to time vary the terms and conditions under which assistance may be given under this section
First we are authorizing the board to give assistance and to majte regulations and determine and vary the method and the kind of assistance which shall be given to each class of people mentioned in the definition of "exporter." Further, in order to make sure

Salt Fish Board
that each and every class, and especially the weaker class, shall be benefited, we have authorized the board under paragraph (c) to act as the agent for the export of the fish put up and prepared by any person who wishes to avail himself of the benefit of that agency. It seems to me that we have provided the basis on which the board may establish regulations to benefit and assist those who want to avail themselves of the provisions of this measure, and we have provided a means whereby the board can give assistance. I admit that specific assistance to each class is not mentioned, but as I said before, that is because of the wide diversity of people that will be entitled to and will claim benefit under the act., and because it will not be possible to establish by statute the form of assistance which may be given under certain circumstances to any set or class of people.
I submit again that we have made this legislation elastic enough to enable the board to help all classes of people, and more particularly the smaller and the weaker man in the set-up, the individual shore fisherman; because the great majority of people who are devoting to this purpose the proceeds of their c-atches are small inshore fishermen, and the intention of the act is well understood by those who know local conditions. I have already stated their understanding of the meaning and purport of this proposed legislation, and the protest which they registered against it, and the attitude of this department.
I will read again, for the benefit of those who did not hear it, the telegram which was sent to me on May 10 by the president of the fisheries committee of the board of trade of Halifax, who is at the same time an exporter of fish in the sense in which the matter is being discussed. The communication reads as follows:
Board of Trade telegram yesterday based newspaper report. Have just seen bill. Definition exporter ambiguous as under definition smallest fisherman becomes exporter if he owns even one pound fish which later is sold to dealer and exported. Actually salt fish exporters are corporation individuals et cetera who conduct or intend conduct more or less regular business of shipping salt fish abroad. Bill mentions board consulting committee on marketing. In addition committee clauses changed as formerly suggested word marketing should be deleted substituting consulting on any matter pertaining to work of board.
Fletcher S. Smith.
These are the words of the exporters, who, it is claimed, stand to benefit most under this act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is not necessarily final. His opinion is not decisive as to the law.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
If it is not necessarily conclusive, it is at least worth while to place it alongside the opinions of those who have expressed the contrary view. This gentleman purports to speak on behalf of the corporation exporters. He objects to the definition which we have given of the word "exporter'r because it will include the smallest fisherman. My reply to that explains my attitude-and the attitude of the government:
Your wire this date received. Do not agree-that definition exporter is ambiguous; on the contrary made for purpose of covering smalt producer. Other suggestions to be taken into consideration. With regard wire yesterday suggestions noted but am afraid cannot be-entertained. The board is to be one for the benefit of the small producer as well as the dealer and exporter.
That was my reply to the gentleman who objected to including in the meaning of "exporter" the small fisherman who puts up only one pound of fish.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the intention of the act is clearly set out in the definition of the word "exporter." subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
We cannot legislate
too directly in this matter. I agree with the minister that we have not absolute jurisdiction, because while we may have jurisdiction *over the fisheries, I do not believe that our jurisdiction extends to the fish once caught. That jurisdiction belongs to the province. Under paragraph (b) of section 6 I believe the board is given a sufficiently wide power. The board may declare, before granting any bonus or assistance to exporters, that they shall raise the price to the fishermen by one-quarter
	*
of a cent or half a cent in order to qualify, and of course the exporters would have to. That would not encroach upon the jurisdiction of the province because the exporters could take advantage of it or not as they saw fit. There is nothing to compel them to come in as there is in Newfoundland.
With regard to the amendment that has been proposed, I do not quite see its purpose. Some hon. members have spoken to me with regard to this particular phase of the bill. It is said that a fisherman might have to wait six months, until the fish which he caught to-day was exported, before he could be subsidized. I do not think that is necessary. In my opinion there is no necessity for an amendment to meet a situation of that kind, because it is provided that the board may give assistance not to exceed in value twenty-five per cent "of the value" of the fish. It does not say, every pound of fish a fisherman caught six months ago or yesterday; it simply says twenty-five per cent of the value of the fish in respect of which such assistance is given. That means salt fish which is to be exported. We can set a value to-day, because there are some exports at the present time. The value in Lunenburg to-day is, I understand, S4.50 a quintal. Suppose the board says the fish is worth only S3; what is there to prevent its fixing that amount? What is there to prevent its saying that the fish is worth $6 and subsidizing on that basis? I cannot see the necessity for the amendment. If a fisherman catches a ton of fish to-day, that fish may be exported six months from now; but the question is, what is the value of exported fish to-day? We do not have to wait six months to find out, because there is to-day a market for export fish. If we were not exporting any fish at all it would be necessary to wait six months to find out what the value was, but we can fix a value to-day, not on the estimate of the board but in accordance with the market. The market price is S4.50 at Lunenburg. If the fisherman catches a ton to-day, why should he wait six months? It is not to that particular ton of fish that this provision applies, but to salt fish to be exported, and therefore we can pay him the twenty-five per cent on that ton of fish right away.

speechtext:
It seems to me we are moving in circles. I regret exceedingly having to be on my feet so many times, but there are so very few in this house who are directly interested in this legislation as representing fishing constituencies that unless we do our duty as we conceive it the fisherman will get no benefit at all. If we cannot do our duty we should not be here. Suggestions have been

Salt Fish Board
made with reference to amending certain sections, but apart from two specific proposals, one in connection with the interpretation clause and the other with regard to the estimate in paragraph (b), nothing definite has been put before the committee. I submit -the suggestion has been made by others- that this board should be an independent body. It should not be made up of exporters; there should not be an exporter on it. If this is the desire and the will of the house, if it is what is fair and reasonable in the interests of all concerned, the fishermen, the exporters and the middlemen, I do not see why the department should relinquish its final authority. As the minister has suggested, the board has power to make recommendations to the governor in council, but I submit that the board should be an independent body. That is point number one. The minister has not intimated that there may not be exporters on the board. If there are [DOT]exporters on it, what business have they to fix the price of fish which they themselves will sell on the market that is available to them?
Another point is this. The poor fisherman, the individual fisherman, the primary producer, is *the man whom we should desire to help. If that is the will of the people, then it should be carried into effect in legislation. It should mot be taken for granted, because I believe it is what is wanted by all classes of our people, irrespective of parties or groups. I know that in the constituency I represent there are very few of the poor fishermen who have sufficient .money to become exporters, and they will be under the lash of the exporter, the man who buys the fish. They will have to sell at his price or not at all. And they cannot sell byproducts. The whole thing is in the hands of the exporters.
A telegram has been read from the chairman of the fisheries committee of the board of trade. With all deference to the Halifax board of trade, I take the responsibility for this statement, having represented that constituency for twenty-five years, that the first interest of the board of trade, or of a large number of members of particular committees [DOT]of the board of trade, is to look after number one, because they are all interested in something or other, whether railways, the transportation board with head office in Moncton, [DOT]or armchair fisheries. From the early days they have gone after the business and now they expect the business to come after them. It is suggested that this legislation is to help the poor fisherman, but, as has been rightly said, these people want to put their heels on the fishermen, those who go out and toil, who take their lives in their hands and sometimes never return. They are afraid the fishermen are going to get something; they are afraid they may become exporters and get a portion of this $800,000. I hope they do; I hope they get the major portion of it.

speechtext: They will not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Certainly they will not. The people who are going to find these markets are the exporters, the men with money in their pockets and money in the bank, who want a little more money. I do not blame them for that; it is only human nature, but they must be protected against themselves and we must protect those who cannot protect themselves. That should be the underlying principle of legislation of this kind. To send this bill from this house to another chamber in its present form, while it does not meet the fair wishes and aspirations of our people, will only bring heartbreak and disappointment to the fishermen who are the primary producers of Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces. No matter in what waters they fish, whether the St. Lawrence, the bay of Chaleur or faraway British Columbia, and whether or not this legislation applies to them directly, the moment you break the hearts of the primary producers of Canada or any other country it is the beginning of the end, and a retrograde move. I am not saying this is necessarily retrograde legislation, but I am trying to point out some of the dangers and some of the shoals. What does the captain do during a fog? He stays on the bridge day and night, looking out for danger. As soon as this legislation is passed the exporter has control, and we shall be helpless until the next session of parliament. So I say it is our duty to see to it that as far as possible this legislation does what we desire. No person is infallible; I am far from infallible, but I never saw such a weak interpretation clause in any bill as we have in this measure. The interpretation clause should be . the governing, all-powerful clause, but it is not; the powerful clause is section 6, which gives this board the power to dispense $800,000 subject to regulations made by the governor in council.

Then there would be some incentive to the poor fisherman, the primary producer, to go

out and catch fish to sell to the exporter. I have lived in or near the city of Halifax all my life and I know all the exporters of fish in that city. There is still another point, Mr. Chairman. I was approached not long ago by a combination of individuals whom I did not even ask to sit down. subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I cannot agree with the minister. There might be a way out of the dilemma for the minister if he could find markets in the western United States, which are nearer to Alberta than eastern Canada is. I do not agree that it is not the responsibility of the department to attempt to help out our coal industry. It is fundamental that the great enterprise in Cape Breton should not be utilized for stockjobbing exploitation by the use of any part of the moneys which we pay in large sums-large sums, mark you!-to assist in employment on that island. This money should not be used to advance the interests and stock-jobbing ambitions of those who have been responsible for some of the happenings which are now before the courts of this country. I give the minister timely warning in order that he may take steps to see that the government is protected by appropriate action, and by doing so he will prevent what I regard as a very serious matter and ensure that these subsidies, heavy as they are, are utilized for the purpose of providing for employment and the development of a fuel policy that will enable this coal from Nova Scotia to be utilized as it now is in the consuming markets of upper Canada.
The minister replied:
My right hon. friend's statement is the first I have heard of the matter. I understand two of the companies mentioned are in financial difficulty or liquidation. I quite agree with the general principle he has enunciated. Certainly I would be the last one in this house to support the payment of public moneys for stockjobbing propositions of any kind.
Mr. Bennett:	I believe that; that is the
reason I bring the matter up here.
Mr. Crerar:	I shall be glad to get some
information in regard to what my right hon. friend has said.

Supply-Mines-Fuel Board

for 1938, particularly at page 653, where there is a statement with regard to these various companies and the values of their stocks at different periods in different years. I traced the corresponding month through three different years, and I was puzzled, after the reference which was made here to stockjobbing operations, at something I found there. I found, for example, that in May, 1933, the price of stock of the Dominion Coal Company was $4 per share; in 1934 it had risen to $81 per share; in May, 1935, it had risen to $138. The high, as at February, 1935, was $140. These subventions were paid largely because of the terrible conditions which existed in the industry in Nova Scotia and because the condition of the miners was desperate. I have not been in Nova Scotia but I have read a great deal in the newspapers about the serious conditions in some of the Nova Scotia mining	areas-for example, at Thorburn,
where I believe a mine was closed and all the people were placed in a position of dire poverty. Are we paying these subventions and subsidies in order that employment may be given and conditions improved for those who work in the mines? If so, I should like to know whether that is being done. I was told that the salaries paid in some of these organizations have been, if they are not now, very high. I understand that the late chairman of the board of the Dominion Coal Company, Sir Newton Moore, who before the war was engaged in the handling of shipments of ore to Germany, was brought over after the war and as chairman received something like $65,000 a year. It occurred to me after I heard that to ask whether these subsidies were really going where the house desires to have them go, namely, for the improvement of the conditions of those who labour in the mining field. An hon. member reminds me that there was a royal commission in Nova Scotia which inquired into the industry, and I would ask the minister whether he looked into the matter, and if so, what his findings were with respect to the statement made last year in this house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT

It may not have been made public. If I understand the hon. member rightly, he takes the position that we should say to the coal companies, "You must do certain things with regard to stock transactions and certain

things with regard to the payment of salaries, or you will not receive any subventions." May I point out again that that is not the basis on which the subvention principle was first established. The principle was established in order to assist the movement of Nova Scotia coal into Ontario, say, to put it on a competitive basis with coal from the United States; and whether the Nova Scotia coal companies producing the coal were earning profits or paying big salaries bore no relation to that question. We could say to the Dominion Coal Company or to any other coal company in Nova Scotia, "You have a good balance sheet and you are earning large profits, therefore we will not pay the subvention." Their reply would be, "Well, we are not going to move coal into Ontario at a loss." The subvention principle is based upon the theory of paying a part of the transportation costs to the consuming point. If we insisted upon trying to give practical effect to the suggestion made, the net result probably would be to throw a good many people out of work in the Nova Scotia mines. So far as my knowledge goes, when the subvention principle was first adopted it was not because the coal companies were in a difficult way in the matter of profits; not at all. It was simply to facilitate the production of more coal in Nova Scotia and to give employment to a greater number of men and to keep them more steadily employed. The officials inform me that this statement is correct.

Suitability
For general steam raising uses in industry, shipping and railways, it is quite satisfactory and the coal produced in the Sydney area is also suitable for coking and gas making; mainland coals are not coking coals.
Supply-Mines-Fuel Board

Unsuitability
Certain industries require a low sulphur coal as the presence of sulphur affects the quality of the product. To mention some: Glass making- brick making-gasworks-and for certain metallurgical purposes.
The low fusion point of a6h is also detrimental when coal is used under heavy forced draft with consequent high furnace temperature, the ash fuses and blocks the air passages in the grate and for furnaces designed for high fusion ash coals Nova Scotia coal is not suitable.
Production
From eight to nine million tons can be produced annually.
Actually, production for the past three five-year periods has been as follows:
From	Net tons
1923-1927	 6,496,000
1928-1932	 6,003,000
1933-1937	 6,104,000
Distribution
The principal markets for Nova Scotia coal are the maritime provinces-Newfoundland- Quebec and Ontario.
Consumption of Coal
Consumption has not remained constant in proportion to business conditions, it is steadily declining in relation to per capita of population.
The decline is in part due to consumers turning to alternative fuels or other sources of energy, also there has been a remarkable trend toward increased efficiencies in the use of coal.
Energy other than coal expressed in equivalent tonnage shows an increase in Canada from 18.592,000 tons in 1927 to 26,432,000 tons in 1936, an increase of nearly 8,000,000 tons or over 40 per cent.
Alternate Fuels
The tendency in recent years is from coal to alternative fuels or energy. As pointed out in the above paragraph, energy other than coal has increased by 40 per cent over the past ten years. Use of coal by Canadian railroads has declined from 10-3 million tons in 1928 to an average in recent years of approximately 6-16 million (40 per cent), while wheat movements and trade activity generally affects traffic volume. The motor driven vehicle competitor has had a serious effect on railway coal consumption, Fuel oil offers some competition not only for steam raising in industry generally but for bunkering and even the heating and cooking market. Hydro-electric power has displaced large tonnages of coal for steam raising.
Economies in the technical use of coal have permitted railways to reduce their consumption by 10 per cent during the past ten years. Similar economies have been achieved in steel manufacture, steam electric power plants and in general steam raising practice.
Importations of Bituminous Coal
Bituminous coal importations for the past five-year period average annually 9,686,000 or li times the present Nova Scotia production, the greater portion of this is used in Ontario.
Quality of importations shows a wide range but such are usually of good quality with low sulphur content-low ash and high fusion of ash.
Preparation is carried out with a great deal of care and coals are sized to meet consumers' demands. Usually the grades sold are screened -run of mine-sized nut and slack.
[Mr. McCulloch.l
Transportation of Nova Scotia Coal Nova Scotia coal receives many handlings before it finally reaches the consumer, which results in a great deal of degradation due to . the friable nature of the coal. It has to move from the mine to loading piers, then from ocean-going boats to terminal storage piles and from that point to railway cars or trucks for final delivery.
Comparison of Prices to Consumer In the province of Quebec, Nova Scotia coal moved by water up the St. Lawrence and distributed from deep water ports can on a price basis compete with imported coal from the United States. Inland movements westward involve a cost which places Nova Scotia coal at a disadvantage with United^ States coal, the greater the distance moved inland from St. Lawrence ports the greater the disadvantage.
Reason for Subventions
Subventions were designed to meet competitive disadvantages and enable Nova Scotia coal to compete with imported coal on an equal price basis, without such assistance it would not be possible for Nova Scotia coal to enter the market west of the island of Montreal.
This aid has been responsible for the movement of nearly twelve million tons of Nova Scotia coal into these competitive markets (as at the end of 1938). In addition to this, some million and a quarter tons of Nova Scotia coal were assisted under the aid of coking legislation.
Production in United States Mines
The United States coal industry is the largest in the world and produces about one hundred times more than the annual output of Nova Scotia with a potential capacity to produce twice the present output. The districts in the United States supplying Canada are Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Qhio and the Virginias, where coal deposits are thick and of excellent quality, they have shallow cover, good roofing conditions and light gradients, they operate with mechanical labour saving equipment, which results in the production per man being about the highest in the world.
It also means that United States bituminous coal is produced at a comparatively low cost and from mines where the shallow cover and easy access simplifies the problems of transportation, ventilation and pumping.
Comparable Conditions in Nova Scotia During the past 100 years the more accessible coal areas in Cape Breton have been worked out and the limited areas now being mined are at points far out under sea and at great depth. Mining in these remote submarine areas entails increasingly large costs of long uphill multiple -systems of haulage and lengthy airways for ventilation,.
Under the land areas seams have been followed to a depth of 4,000 feet, complicating the extraction of coal by heavy gradients representing high power costs for haulage and pumping.
Production per man employed in Nova Scotia is on the average 2-2 tons per day compared with 4-5 tons in the United States field.
Mechanization of Mines (U.S.)
In southern Pennsylvania, Kentucky and Virginia, production per man actually runs up to 10 tons per day with the_ greatly increased mechanization of mines. This mechanization is on the increase, which will still further intensify

Supply-Mines-Fuel Board
competition. One mine in West Virginia is now planning to produce 6,552 tons per day with 500 men, equivalent to 13 tons per man per day.
Mechanization of Mines (N.S.)
Nova Scotia operators are endeavouring to keep apace by extending the use of this labour saving machinery. Coal cutting machinery was introduced in the mines many years ago, and the system of handling coal by conveyer belts has been done for some fifteen years.
Further progress is hoped for but the term mechanization includes a complete cycle by which coal is cut-bored-loaded and hauled mechanically to the tipple. The physical conditions of the Nova Scotia mines do not in every case lend themselves to complete mechanization. Where it is possible operators are endeavouring to use the most modern mining equipment.
In one instance equipment for the complete mechanization of a mine was purchased at a cost of some $400,000. It was installed and tried out but local labour refused to operate it, claiming its use would displace manual labour and also that it was unsafe; the mine is still idle with the equipment still there.
As a matter of fact this installation would not have displaced any labour as it is a new mine. It might eventually reduce the number of men employed for the same tonnage but by increasing the tons per man employed reduces cost of operation, thereby making extension of markets possible. Mining coal by old fashioned methods is too costly and to compete in consuming markets modern mining methods must be pursued.
Capacity to Produce
There is what is known as producers and non-producers in every mine. Producers are engaged at the coal face, actually mining coal, and non-producers are made up of men employed in handling coal from face to bankhead, maintenance of mine, preparation of the coal, and finally loading into cars.
In Nova Scotia coal mining 38 per cent of the men employed are producers and 62 per cent non-producers. American mines, with which Nova Scotia coal competes, have 60 per cent producers and 40 per cent non-producers.
The reason is that in Nova Scotia a large proportion of non-producers are required to meet the adverse conditions previously set out re:-
(1)	Distance from face to tipple with steep gradients.
(2)	Great depth of cover with heavy roof costs.
(3)	Comparatively thin seams.
(4)	Gasey and dusty mines, long and costly airways which restrict the free use of electricity, which is an important factor.
Regarding (1) loss in effective working time underground amounts to 1 hour 20 minutes per shift due to the time required for the workmen to travel from pit to face and return.
Also, steep gradients and gaseous conditions do not permit the extensive use of electric locomotives which play an important part in low cost production in United States areas.
Ventilation is also extremely costly in the submarine workings, necessitating in some instances coursing air for nine miles entailing large power consumption.
Marketing Handicaps
The Cape Breton collieries producing 80 per cent of the coal are dependent upon water transportation during the summer months. The St. Lawrence movement represents 60 per cent of the total production of Cape Breton, requiring peak loads for labour during the season of navigation with a serious slackening off during winter months.	,
Then again, coal produced during the winter months must be banked in readiness for summer movement. Similarly, the coal brought up during the summer has to be banked at terminals for winter delivery. This extra handling and storage, combined with weathering and the friable nature of the coal causing slackening and deterioriation in size, adds considerably to the cost. Much United States coal is delivered direct from the mines to consumer without this additional heavy cost burden.
Always to be borne in mind is the effect upon industry of increased coal prices. In the iron and steel industry it means 30 per cent of the cost of production and about 25 per cent in the manufacture of cement. Put the price of coal beyond that of competing fuels and you lose that market immediately.

As I stated the other night, it would be quite possible but extremely improbable to have a coal policy-some people talk about the need for a coal policy, a rather general term-whereby subventions would be increased to the point to enable every Canadian coal consumer, whether it be a manufacturing establishment or a domestic consumer, to be supplied with Canadian coal. But that could be done only at greatly increased cost either to the federal treasury or to the industries and domestic consumers which were using the coal. After all, in the application of this principle regard must be had for all the factors and considerations involved. I am not saying that the subvention policy is sound or unsound, all I say is that it was initiated for a particular purpose and, so far as my knowledge goes, it has been applied effectively through the years to meet that purpose.

They are doing good not only to Nova Scotia and Alberta and British . Columbia but to the areas through which the coal moves. They are paid by way of reduction in freight rates, or under some conditions a lump sum is allotted to a company, but it is based on the freight rates. Therefore very little of the subventions

which is expended on the movement of coal from Nova Scotia is expended in that province; it is spent in Quebec, in Ontario, where the coal is consumed, or in the areas through which it moves. That is a point to be borne in mind. The subvention is not paid as a bonus on the production of coal.
Some hon. members have referred to comparative costs of mining coal. Certainly there is a marked difference in the cost of coal in Nova Scotia and in Alberta. But it must be remembered that almost all the coal of Nova Scotia is taken from subterranean areas which are costly to maintain. If hon. members saw some of the timber which goes into Nova Scotia mines to keep up the roofs they would think it was a pulp mill rather than a coal mine. The amount of wood which goes into the mines is enormous. Also a great number of steel girders are used; in some instances they are very close together. They protect the roofs of the main parts of the mine. There are miles on miles of these iron girders, and they are very expensive. I do not know their cost to-day, but formerly it cost over $5 apiece to put them in place; that is just for the labour to put up a girder, not counting the cost of the material. I know of instances where men got more than $5 apiece for erecting these girders. WThen one is talking about cost one must bear in mind the varying conditions under which coal mines are operated.
Apart from the discussion which we have heard this afternoon, in my opinion there are some vital points which the minister of the department should take under consideration. The remarks I am about to make have special reference to my own constituency of Cape Breton South and the constituencies surrounding it. I do not profess to speak for any area other than the one I represent. In Cape Breton South we have at least two districts where the resources of coal have become depleted. One is at a place called Reserve. Conditions there are very bad for the reason that for soipe years only a very small quantity of coal has been taken out, although the quality is excellent; I believe that no better coal is mined in Canada. However, after producing for a great number of years, the resources have become depleted and the community which has been built up round that particular place is in serious difficulties.
What I have in mind is this. The Minister of Agriculture has the authority to declare a national emergency in respect of sections which are drought-stricken or insect-ridden or afflicted with some like calamity. Coal mining is just as basic an industry as wheat or lumber or fishing. Perhaps the Minister of

Supply-Mines-Fuel Board
Mines and Resources could use his good offices to have a locality like Reserve declared to be in a condition of national emergency as regards the basic industry, and work out, in cooperation with the Department of Labour, some method of alleviating the financial conditions of those people and securing work for them. In the Reserve district there is a seam of coal which is called the Emery seam. It has not been worked, and I do not know whether it is financially feasible to work it, but I suggest that the minister endeavour to have the company investigate the possibility of the immediate opening up of the Emery seam, if necessary with federal assistance, to give employment to the people of that district.
In another section of Cape Breton South, namely the Broughton district, we had at one time four mines. They were worked on what they call the top basin seam; that is, there was a basin all round. As time went on, all the mines had to be closed. There is quite a large population in Broughton, and it is in the heart of the coal district-not the mining area but the coal district. Mines were operated there a great many years ago. I maintain that some consideration should be given to the matter of opening a mine in order to give work to the people of that district. I may be asked, how are we going to do it?
We need a subvention to get our coal to a good market and overcome our other disabilities. We are placed, I suggest, in a peculiar position compared with every other basic industry in the dominion. I was in favour of a fixed price for wheat, and I have backed the western members all the way through because I think the idea is a good one; I am not criticizing the wheat interests or the action which has been taken for their preservation. But, I say, we are placed in a different position; for while Canada produces more wheat than she can sell, apparently our coal mines cannot produce more than half of what Canada can consume. As a matter of fact we produce only half of Canada's bituminous coal consumption; about 17,000,000 tons are imported against 17,000,000 tons produced in the dominion. That throws a different light on the coal business in Canada. While that condition obtains, while we cannot produce nearly enough coal to supply our Canadian needs, there must be some way to remedy the condition of the coal mining industry.
I know that everybody criticizes the minister, the department and the government. I do not want to do that, but I should like to offer one or two suggestions which might
be adopted with satisfactory results. One is that the fuel board should be given the powers of a marketing board. I believe that in that way a great deal of good could be done. Then, as the effect of our subvention is to bring down the price of our coal to the competitive price of the imported article, I cannot see why the railroads, on the basis of competition, with prices the same as between imported and home-produced coal, would not purchase our Canadian coal. If the fuel board were a marketing board, or if the railways had power to import coal and sell it, then all our Canadian coal could be taken over at a price which would afford the producer a margin with which to carry on his operations. All our Canadian coal could be so disposed of and we could import from the United States the coal necessary to make up the deficiency. Then the price could be adjusted, and I venture to say that on the total transaction the railways concerned would make from 85 cents to $1 a ton, which might go a long way towards absorbing a large proportion, if not all, of the deficit of the government-owned transportation system. This, I suggest, is worth wffiile taking into consideration. These are two constructive suggestions, but I say -and I mean this-that so far the principle of coal subventions based upon the tonnage rate has been the best coal policy we have had. This does not mean, of course, that we must stop there and not make efforts to improve conditions; for, while we are importing coal because we are unable to sell coal that could be produced in Canada, there is something wrong. We must be able to take up the slack, and if we had an outlet for 1,500,000 or 2,000,000 tons more of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick coal there would be no distress whatever in that part of the dominion.
I greatly sympathize with the minister; I am sure he must be getting weary of all these useless questions and all the explanations he has to make with regard to subventions. Some question, has been raised as to what control the government exercises. Clause 10 of the order in council provides that assistance shall not be granted to those, otherwise eligible to participate, who refuse or fail to furnish such information as the Minister of Mines and Resources may consider necessary in the administrative duties connected with this movement; that for the purpose of certifying such information the minister, or such officers of the dominion fuel board as he may designate, shall have free access to all books, records, and so forth kept by shippers or the railways in connection with
Supply-Min c &-Fuel Board

this movement, and that he may make such examination thereof as shall be deemed necessary or expedient. The government has always maintained full control as to the payment of subventions, to whom and when they shall be paid, and so on, and there is no question in the minds of the Nova Scotia miners about the help these subventions have provided. They have aided1 our industry remarkably, and we hope they will be of still greater assistance in the future.
Last year a good many of us were caught off our guard. The year 1937 had been such a good one in the coal trade that it was not until June that we realized we were in a tail spin, as a result of conditions in the United States, which brought about a slowing down of operations in our pulp mills. These mills have always used a considerable amount of our coal, and it was not until June that we realized we were in this tail spin. The result was three or four months of a bad fall and winter for us. I am satisfied, however, that, remedial measures having been taken, there will be a considerable improvement in the province and that conditions will be far better than they have ever been in the coal industry there.
There are two or three extraneous factors to he taken into consideration. One of them does not depend upon Canada at all. If the United States would put into force an act similar to the Guffey act for the regulation of the sale of "distress coal" in that country, that would be one of the biggest boosts our coal industry could get. To-day there are unorganized mines in the United States shipping in a great volume of bootlegged coal, but we cannot very well do anything about it without disturbing our entire system of subventions and tariffs as it affects the United States, but I believe the time will come when the United States Senate will have to take some action to organize the coal industry there and to provide that coal shall not be sold below a certain price. While the Guffey act was in force conditions were a good deal better, but the moment it was declared ultra vires we began to suffer. That is one of the factors affecting our coal industry, but I am hoping that legislation similar to this will be reintroduced in the United States.
One thing more. We all realize that economic conditions in Canada are improving, and this means that economic conditions will improve in our province especially in the pulp and paper industry so that we shall sell a great deal more coal than we have done in the past.

I am not opposing subventions. As I have said, I will support the subventions; I will support the proposal of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) that we pay the primary producer of fish a reasonable and

The question was: During the recess did the minister get that information? We are not opposed to subventions, but I think the committee will agree that before the dominion government pays out money to any industry or for any purpose it should know exactly where that money is going. I intend to refer very briefly to this report. First it gives the financial set-up of the Acadia Coal Company, as follows: the first preferred stock, amounting to $1,900,000, is all owned by the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, Limited. The second preferred stock, amounting to $1,000,000, is also owned by the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, with the exception of $5,500. The common stock, totalling $1,846,100, is almost all owned by the same company. On the other hand all the common stock of the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, amounting to $15,000,000, was owned by the British Empire Steel Corporation and later by its successor, the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. This information appears at page 8 of the report. On page 10 I find the following:
Schedule "C" indicates some rather startling facts. In 1925 when the loss of Acadia is shown to be $128,469.66, the Scotia Company took from Acadia cash to the amount of $1,591,921.21. In 1932 when the loss of Acadia is shown to be $180,174.38, the Scotia Company obtained from Acadia the sum of $724,895.87 cash; and on the 19th of January, 1933, the day that the receiving order was granted against Scotia, that company received from Acadia the sum of $20,000 cash, and on that day the memorandum shows that The Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company owed Acadia Coal Company a total of $1,703,410.81.

I have only a few words to say in connection with this item. Before the six o'clock recess I was reading from the report of the royal commission on the Acadia Coal Company. The commissioners made definite findings in regard to holding companies, and from those findings I shall read briefly:
It cannot be said, having regard to all the facts, that from 1925 until January, 1933, the affairs of Acadia were conducted or managed in the best interests of the company, or in the interests of the industry in Pictou county. There was nothing illegal from the point of view of authority in the various matters of borrowing and dividend payments already mentioned. In fact it cannot be said there was anything illegal in those transactions from any point of view. Legality of action, however, is one thing, and preserving and safeguarding the industry and all that that implies is quite another thing. It is, therefore, the considered view of your commissioners that some legislative action should be taken in regard to the powers of holding companies. Some restrictions should be placed on their present powers, especially in the matter of dealing with subsidiary companies. A holding company in control of the common stock of another company has absolute power over its destiny, notwithstanding that the public own the actual property through mortgage bonds and debenture stock. A holding company may through bad management plunge its subsidiary into debt, but may not be responsible for the liquidation of that debt, and thus the property of the real owners may be sacrificed. There is no intention to suggest here that any action should be taken which would unduly interfere with the status quo, or any action which in the remotest way would be calculated to disrupt business; but it is thought that restrictions and limitations may be imposed which would cure an undoubted existing evil, and there does not seem to be any reason for confirming any such restrictions to companies which deal with the public assets of the province, such as coal operations, lumber operations, or operations of water power.
We are here dealing with the payment of public money to an industry for a specific purpose. The purpose is that of enabling the industry to sell its product in a competitive market where it could not sell without that assistance, in order that by so doing it may give employment to a larger number of workers. All we are asking here is that the government should exercise that control which is necessary to see that the purpose for which the subsidy or subvention is paid is being carried out.

Anyone who has visited the coal mining areas of Nova Scotia will realize the amount of destitution and misery which exists in those areas, while the people who have been manipulating the mines have been living in the greatest luxury. That is a condition which in my opinion we should not allow to continue, and something which cannot continue without having far-reaching economic and political effects on the life of the country. Before the house meets again to deal with an estimate of this kind, I think the minister should have more information in the matter than he now has.

In some instances a mine may be operating a considerable distance from railway transportation. subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: With the minister's interest in the development of mining properties and the creation of employment, I wonder if he will not have a chat with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) for the purpose of seeing if some of this money cannot be used to create employment for the innumerable silver miners who are now out of employment. There are very many silver properties in the Slocan district which are closed because the price of silver does not warrant operation. The Minister of Labour thinks it is a matter for the Minister of Finance; the Minister of Finance thinks it is a matter of government policy and that assistance is hardly warranted from a financial point of view. But these miners make the proposal that the government assist them only on such silver producing properties as were opened in 1939, and they ask for that assistance by way of an increased price of silver. But it does not necessarily have to be an increased price of silver. It can be assistance in any way the government pleases, just the same kind of assistance, if they like, that they have been giving to salt fish, cheese, coal mines and so forth. The government is not asked to put out one dollar until these men have put in a good deal of preliminary work and have incurred preliminary expenses in exploring, drilling and so on, and with all this money to spend it does seem that it would be practicable for the government to encourage the development of these new properties, thereby putting many men to work. The minister says that 30,000 men were given employment by the opening up of new properties last year through the assistance given in mining operations. That number might be materially added to if assistance were given to these silver producing properties. There is no expenditure asked to be made by the government until these miners have first spent their efforts and their money in finding new properties and opening them up.

For a minister of mines who is so extremely' placid in his temperament, the minister shows a little bit of warmth about this matter, and I am afraid that I am putting my finger more or less on the spot.
I am not objecting to the building of this road, but certainly it is not being built primarily for the development of mining, as set forth in this vote, and as very candidly set forth by the minister in the early part of the evening. The idea of giving grants to provincial governments to get trails or roads to mines is a principle we all endorse, provided it stimulates mining output and assists the pioneer developer of mines in getting his property developed. But the mining area at Finlay Forks is a long way from Vanderhoof. If the minister would second the assistance and knowledge of the hon. member for the district, and if he in turn would be thoroughly candid about the matter and tell the committee of the controversy as between the Monkman pass route and this route, we should get pretty near the truth.
I think the vote for this route which is being paid for out of this appropriation ought to be paid for, as assistance to roads in different parts of the country is paid for, as a direct grant for the relief of unemployment. To bring it under this vote is stretching the thing to the limit. I do not know of any vote in the estimates whereunder the Monk-man route can be properly discussed. I do not believe that there is a vote here where we would be any more in order in discussing it than under this vote. The Monkman route from the Peace River section of Alberta into British Columbia is undoubtedly the right one for the opening up of transportation facilities from the Peace river down to the coast; the people of that district have gone ahead and made a road for a considerable distance, over which they have managed to travel; in fact a car came through, with great difficulty, last fall; but the enterprise and

Supply-Mines-Geology
the sacrifice of the people on that route in spending their own money and labour and time upon it deserve recognition. It is a much better and a much shorter route than this one; and personally I regard it as a mistake and as unfair to the committee to designate the appropriation to the Finlay Forks district as an appropriation in the interests of the development of mining, because it is nothing of the kind. True, there is some mining, and some very important mining, in there, particularly at Finlay Forks, which is a long way up; and in the Ingenika some very old silver lead properties, as well as the placer properties the minister has mentioned, have been operated for years.
I am all in favour of rendering assistance in opening up roads over long distances into new territories, but I do not think the committee should be, I will not say misled, but led into the impression that this is strictly devoted to the purpose set forth in the appropriation in the sense in which the minister explained the appropriation in the early part of the evening. We also ought to recognize that these routes are a matter of controversy, and very bitter controversy, in that whole district, and there is a.great deal of resentment and ill feeling in that the government, while able to spend a large sum last year-I should like the minister to tell me the amount, but I will venture the figure of $100,000-upon the road from Vanderhoof to Finlay Forks, has refused any recognition of the magnificent efforts of the settlers on the route from the Peace River country to Fort George. To question this is, to say the least, stretching the credulity of members of this committee to about the breaking point.

That was the impression he left; there is no question about it; and he mentioned that there was some good mining beyond Finlay Forks, which is some distance beyond Vanderhoof. But he did not notice-if he had he would have been honest enough to inform the committee-that the road on this side of Finlay Forks has not only been opened up but has been developed and has proved one of the best mining districts in British Columbia, the employment having increased from seventy-five men in the maximum mining season in 1936, when the money was first spent, to 615 privately employed workers in 1937. The same number were employed in 1938, but there will not be as many in 1939 because a good deal of the preliminary work has been done. There will still be, however, hundreds of men employed for nearly two seasons. Winter camps were opened in the district north of Fort St. James and south of Finlay Forks for the first time in the history of British Columbia, and the hon. member for Kootenay East, who represents a mining district, ought to be aware

of that. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) is not supposed to know. That hon. gentleman, in every session since 1936, has asked formal questions as to what, if any, mining development has been taking place along that route. He evidently forgets that two years ago he asked a series of questions which were answered by the department indicating what mining development is going on. Perhaps it will do some good and put a stop to controversy, because there is no clash of opinion as between the proposed Monkman pass highway and this one-none whatever. Those men and women who have been doing voluntary work on the Monkman pass deserve every possible credit.

Yes, it is mining. I can say to the committee that the Monkman Pass Highway Association has a branch in the town of Prince George, British Columbia, of which the mayor of that town, Mr. A. M. Patterson, is chairman. There is also a branch of the highway association in the city of Vancouver. All these branches are active, and the people throughout the entire Peace River country have demanded the construction of this highway. Up to the present time it has not been considered necessary to mention the many resolutions, petitions and similar statements presented by people throughout that district demanding the construction of this highway. The hon. member for Cariboo and the minister must know as well as I do that petitions and resolutions by the dozen and by the score have been showered upon them advocating the construction of this highway. Why? Because not more than five per cent of the total combined population of northern British Columbia and northern Alberta will be served by the route upon which the money is now being spent. In other words, in order to benefit five per cent of the people we have allowed the other ninety-five per cent to go by the board. That is why we say there is a clash of opinion. Just as soon as assistance is given the Monkman pass highway project the government will find the people of the Peace River country earnestly desiring to help any other road the government may wish, so long as those people believe they are given fair play, which they do not think they are receiving from the government at the present time.
A moment ago I said I would be very glad to pass over to the minister a map which I hold in my hand showing the location of the proposed Monkman pass highway, together with a tracing showing the so-called Turgeon route from Fort St. James to Manson Creek and on to Finlay Forks. We have been told from time to time that it would be necessary to undertake various surveys of the Monkman pass route, but may I point out to the minister that last year and the year before the people of the Peace River country, on their own

Supply-M ines-Geology
initiative and iby their own efforts, without the assistance of a single dollar from any municipal, provincial or federal government, undertook to build the highway themselves. That is something which, so far as I know, has not been equalled anywhere else in Canada.
It shows that they really want this route, and surely the determination shown indicates the sincerity of their desire. To them this means an outlet much shorter than by any other proposed route. First of all we want an outlet; then, if it is found necessary to help out the mining areas, no one will object to that. I think it is my duty to place on record an expression of the sentiments held by the Monkman Pass Highway Association, and to point out the vast number of people who belong to that organization and the huge territory it covers. They urge:
1.	Without the assurance of a coast outlet the settlement of the Peace River territory would never have been accomplished. Construction on what was to be a through line of the C.N.R. through Whitecourt was already under way when settlers came over the 270 miles from Edson and the 500 miles by way of Slave Lake and Athabasca.
2.	Repeated promises that this outlet would be constructed as soon as financially possible have supported all further settlement and development. Project after project of less real importance is being financed and this outlet is still denied.
3.	At present the Peace River is considered the most remote from markets, and transportation the most costly of any district in Canada. With its proper outlet it would be one of the closest.
4.	An outlet is essential to any further development. Any increase in population must be on the wooded or sub-marginal lands. This is impossible if to the cost of clearing and of building up the poorer soils must be added the existing handicap of transportation.
5.	The tourist situation is unfair. To support what is becoming one of the greatest industries in Canada the government is spending greater sums each year. We are paying our share of this burden but are denied any possible chance of benefit. By the comparatively trifling expenditure on this connecting link of 150 miles enormous tourist opportunities would be offered of benefit not only to the Peace River country but to the whole dominion.	*
So far as the road itself is concerned, it is the most direct, most feasible and easiest built highway to provide an outlet for the people of the Peace River country. They have this project at heart; they have done all kinds of work on their own initiative in order to further it, and I think in fairness to them some encouragement and recognition should be shown by this government through some grant or donation at least to match what we have done for the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and other such corporations.

I had intended also to refer to various resolutions passed by Liberal organizations throughout the Peace River country, copies of which have been sent to me, but we have followed the principle of not dragging in politics in regard to this question. It is not a political matter; it is a question of justice alone. The people of that country have been promised this outlet, and that promise has not been kept. Now we see large sums of money being spent elsewhere, so it is no wonder a clash of opinion has developed, as the hon. member for Cariboo has said. But 'let me assure the minister that there is no difference of opinion as to what route should be constructed. The clash of opinion is simply this: We do not want to see this much money spent on another road while the Monkman pass highway receives no recognition. In all fairness to the people of the Peace River constituency I feel that some provision should be made, even at this late stage, in order to assist in putting this road through. It gives me great pleasure to forward this well drawn map to the Minister of Mines and Resources so that he may have a clear idea of the project that is proposed.

While I have no Indians in my riding, except those who might be on the white Indian list if it is still maintained in the province, nevertheless for a number of years I have been deeply interested in the whole Indian situation in Canada. During the past few years I have had the pleasure of having several Indian guides with me on extensive journeys over unsettled country and up and down the rivers and lakes, and I have become greatly interested in them. I had the good fortune on more than one occasion of having a talk with the late Chief Grey Owl, whose name we see frequently in the press even to-day. In the course of these travels I have traversed quite a number of the reserves, and I am happy to say that I have noticed an increase under the present minister in the department's activities among the Indians. Perhaps I should not go out of my way to throw him too many bouquets, but I have come across his tracks on more than one trip. I have been pleased with his interest in the Indians, and I am satisfied that he is doing his best. However, there is a very great deal of improvement to be made.
I have long wondered, recalling that the North American Indians in former years produced such men as Brant, Red Jacket, Tecum-seh and other famous chiefs and great men capable of negotiating with the whites and taking care of their own affairs, why it is that in these later days, after association with the whites for generation after generation, our Indians apparently are unable to take care of themselves even as successfully as those whom we call black men in South Africa and the coloured races elsewhere. Why is it that the

Indians, who have been taken care of by the government and treated more or less as children, are apparently unable to go out and take care of themselves?

I believe that in the
United States considerable efforts have been made on behalf of the Indians in the last few years. I have made quite an investigation in many state capitals where there are Indian branches. They have been trying to elevate the Indian and have made, I believe, important progress in that direction.
All I have to say on this subject I will say in relation to these three items dealing with Indian welfare, medicine and education.
On some of the reservations there are hospitals. The one at Oshweken, in the Six Nations reservation, is doing splendid work. The doctors and nurses give good value for every dollar which is spent there. Comparing the medical care and attention given on the Six Nations reservation and on the next reserve west, the Muncey reservation, I find this difference. Indians, both mothers and fathers, love their children, if possible more intensely than do white parents; when the children have to leave the Muncey reserve and go to a hospital at London or in that neighbourhood for medical or hospital attention, the parents fret far more than is necessary; and whatever member of their family is away at the hospital is no less distracted at having to be absent from home. On the other hand on the Six Nations reservation, as the parents are in close touch with their children when in hospital, and can go to them in a very short time, there is not the same distraction as occurs on the reservations where there are no hospitals. So it would be a great help to them if the department could provide money to build even a small hospital on a reservation. It would be better in every way for the Indians. It is said that many parents whose children may be slightly affected with tuberculosis keep them at home rather than send them some distance to a hospital. I hope that the minister will find the time and money to arrange for the equipment of the larger reserves with hospitals, somewhat after the style and with the equipment of the one at Oshweken. In northern Ontario, where I have been a great deal in the past few years, I find that sick Indians have to be sent a hundred or a hundred and fifty miles away; there is a marked absence of hospital facilities on the reserves.
With regard to the educational system in vogue in Canada for the instruction of the Indians, I do not know that it is the best.

In the United States practically all the schools are under the federal government. I am not referring unkindly to religious or denominational education institutions-for these do good work-when I say that in the whole of the United States there are probably not more than twenty-four such Indian schools, with 2,000 pupils, whereas 26,000 Indian children go to schools operated by the government; and I am told over there that the latter type of education has been found to be better-I do not know whether that is the case or not. Nor do I know whether the schools we have in Canada are getting better results than those of the United States, but our neighbours must have some reason for placing the education of the Indian children largely under the federal government.
