speechtext: No. Most of the Indian children in this country are educated at denominational institutions. I have been to a number of them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: They get the federal grant.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
They get the federal grant, but I am speaking of their being under the control of the federal government. I do not know which is the better system, but I say that in the south they follow the system of public education by the government.
The children educated in our schools are taught all kinds of domestic science, and, among other things, nursing. I know of a case where a young woman who had been sent away to be trained as a nurse found, when she came home, that there was no nursing for her to do on the reservation. White nurses were used exclusively. I hope the minister will be able to develop a system whereby Indian girls trained as nurses can be given employment at reservation hospitals; at least, at those hospitals devoted to the care of Indians. I do not mean that there should not be any white nurses, but consideration should be given to the employment of a certain number of Indian nurses at institutions to which Indians go for medical attention.
The same consideration applies to schools. When these children go home, to what do they go? I went to one reservation and found that a veiy bright young woman had just come back from an Indian training school. She came to a cottage or hut ten feet bj? twelve feet. Her father and mother and the three or four other members of the family lived in that small hut. Under such conditions these young people will merely revert to what they were before they went away
170S

Supply-Mines-Indian Affairs
Surely the department can develop some system whereby Indian children, at least those trained in the residential schools, can have a better place to go than to return to a hut ten feet by twelve and to the conditions which apply in a place of that description.
Another thing I found was that a great deal of the territory formerly hunted over by the Indians is being over-run. Take northern Ontario from Sudlbury west and north of lake Nipigon, east and west along the Albany river, east andi west along the Ogoki river, from Nipigon south; that whole territory, which was formerly a hunting ground of the Indians, is over-run by whites. What are the Indians going to do when once that territory is settled? Whites are travelling all through that country, and when they come to a hunting ground or a place where the Indians have traps they chase the Indians away. I do not know why the Indians do not maintain their traps. I have thought at different times that surely there is some way to employ the Indian more effectively by teaching him more than he learns in the schools. Are the young Indians taught how to handle and understand outboard motors, or rather are they thoroughly trained in the operation of outboard motors? Some of the guides I have had with me were splendid guides, but when the outboard motor got out of condition they had to paddle, sometimes a long distance. I think the government owes something to the young Indian guide. Indians make splendid guides. I trust myself to them on the most dangerous rivers, and they are absolutely reliable and entirely honest.	.
It has also occurred to me that while the government, to encourage the fine young fellows, gives them badges, after an Indian has performed service as a guide for five years he might 'be given, in addition to the badge, a star and bar like a railway conductor wears, and after a further five years another star could be awarded. They take a great pride in meriting any little courtesy shown them. These guides deserve consideration, and I hope the minister will consider the suggestion. The minister said something about treaty money. I suggest that when Indians receive treaty money no one should be allowed on the reservation except government officials and the Indians themselves, because certain white people-I will not characterize them any more fully-flock to the Indian reservations when they know that treaty money has been received, and they are usually able to find out. I do not think sales agents should be
[Mr. MacNicol.l
allowed to go there such times. Let the Indians spend the money as they see fit, and not on cheap jewellery sold at high prices.
With reference to the Oshweken or Six Nations band, who are perhaps more advanced than other bands of Indians in the more settled part of the country, I would urge upon the minister the importance of properly housing the historic relics that are scattered all through that district. I came across some excellent relics in Brantford'-a good place for them-and among other things I saw a beautiful sash given by the Indians to the daughter of the Indian agent, the head of the reservation, at the time of the Duke of Connaught's visit years ago. It is highly prized. I wonder if the department would consider erecting a small museum at Oshweken, Brant county, in which could be gathered together all these Indian relics, which in due course will be lost to the country unless some effort is made to collect and preserve them.
In conclusion, I believe the minister is doing the best he can, and I wish him every success in his efforts further to elevate the standards of the Indians.

speechtext: I wish to say a word for my fellow Indians; for I am one of them, having been honoured by reception into a glorious clan during the past summer, just after the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) received his degrees. The two schools I visited at lake Nipigon were as fine as anything I expect to see in the way of education, and the community work there is highly commendable. I saw forty young folks digging potatoes a,nd having a happy time looking after the digging machines. Our agent there is a man of outstanding ability, and when their majesties visited the head of the lakes they were surprised at the display put on. It was no doubt a stepping-stone to the great exhibition at Calgary where his majesty was made honorary chief. I congratulate the minister on his work and the work of our agent at the head of the lakes. We believe we have a first-class man. I hope that the good work done in hospitalization will be kept up.

speechtext: I would draw the minister's attention to serious allegations made in British Columbia by medical men and by the provincial minister of health, who has publicly stated that Ottawa does hamper the treatment of tuberculosis in that province. They say that the grant given by the dominion does not begin to scratch the surface, pointing out that 2,600 active cases were tabulated last year. The minister may be increasing the appropriation this year. Is that a fact? I think the seriousness of the charge should be brought to his attention and something more than has been done so far should be undertaken.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The year before last we
started with a small vote looking to the treatment of tuberculosis among the Indians. Last year the appropriation was $250,000, and this year we propose to spend about $300,000. That is to be divided among the Indian population in the various provinces. I am not in a position to say what share of that will go to British Columbia. It will be a substantial portion, because there are more than 25,000 Indians in that province. The approach to the problem of handling tuberculosis among the Indians has been first through the schools. Surveys have been made of the residential schools and the children found to be infected
have been segregated in order to prevent the spread of the disease to healthy children. As our funds permitted, these surveys were made in order to get a general cross-section of the tuberculosis condition on some reserves, and in some instances sanatorium treatment was provided.
I can say quite frankly that this aspect of the medical problem among our Indians is serious, and only within the last two or three years has any particular attention been paid to the question of a program looking to the eradication of tuberculosis among the Indians in much the same way that this is being done in the various provinces for the white population. I can say, however, that in developing and carrying out such a program we have had the benefit of the advice of the medical authorities of each province charged with the handling of the tuberculosis problem among the white population, and here I should like to pay a tribute of thanks to them; they have been most helpful in every way possible. But I would emphasize to the committee that at the moment we are really laying down a line of attack on this problem so far as the Indians are concerned, and it may well be that within the next year or two we shall have to ask for larger appropriations for this purpose.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Does the minister mean that all this work has been done in connection with the Indians of British Columbia, or has some of it been done in connection with the Indians of the Georgian bay district, for instance? There are some reserves in the Georgian bay area, and I would ask what has been done for them.

I am sorry to say that in some instances the percentage ran pretty high. I am told that a survey was made of Manitoulin island, but at the moment I have not before me the results of that survey.

speechtext:
I had in mind that a great deal of money is spent and a good deal of work done by the people who have summer homes and who belong to clubs in the Georgian bay district. There is one Indian village just south of Moose point. I do not know where they get their money, but I know the taxes on their properties are very high. I am not aware that any money has been spent there by the dominion govern-
Supply-Mines-Indian Affairs

meat, either in connection with schools or in connection with medical services. I remember that last year I asked the Minister of Transport if he would not put a few more buoys in that part of Georgian bay-

No, largely for
the benefit of the Indians. The summer people who go there do a great deal for the Indians, and I am just wondering how much of this money is spent by the government in that area south of Moose point, at Parry's island and Beausoleil.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I should like to express my commendation of the efforts made by the government during the last two or three years towards eradicating tuberculosis among the Indians. I represent perhaps the largest reserve in Canada, and I have seen the wonderful interest taken and the effort made by the Indians to free themselves of this dreaded disease. I believe the department has been very wise in the method it has followed in the expenditure of public money for this purpose, in endeavouring to cooperate with the local sanatoriums. In the city of Brantford we have a sanatorium well equipped for this treatment which has one ward very little used, which I believe they are prepared to make available to the Indian department to assist in the treatment of this disease. In that area we. have some 5,000 Indians surrounded by whites, and naturally we realize the importance of helping to keep those Indians healthy, because, after all, if they are not healthy they jeopardize the health of the white people. Of course we should not look at the matter only from the point of view of the interest of the whites; the Indians are a race worthy of being maintained. They have made and can still make a great contribution to the national life of this country. I believe this government, and particularly the Minister of Mines and Resources, have done a great deal to free the Indians of this terrible disease, and I have seen the result of these efforts right in my own locality. I believe the fact that the department is cooperating with the local institutions will ensure that we get the greatest possible value for the public money which is spent in this way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I am sorry I cannot give the hon. member for St. Paul's the detailed information for which he asks. I can say this, that the total amount expended in Ontario last year for the survey of Indian schools and Indian children was $4,811. I should add that this work is carried on in cooperation with the authorities in the provinces, and as
	.
I said a moment ago they have been most helpful in providing the facilities and, in many instances, the technicians necessary for the X-ray work and that sort of thing. That cooperation-and I may say we have received it in every province-has enabled the department to perform a great deal more work than otherwise would have been possible with the amount of money at our disposal. speechtext: The Indian settlements in the Georgian bay district add much to the tourist trade in that area. Private citizens who have camps round there have been generous in their gifts towards the eradication of tuberculosis. Having in mind the advantage of maintaining those Indians, so far as the tourist trade and their usefulness to Canada are concerned, I think special consideration should be given to the matter. In addition to the pecuniary advantages to be derived, we must not lose sight of the humanitarian side of the question, because the Indians suffer great hardships. I should like to see more funds allocated next year to the care of the Indians in the Georgian bay district.

speechtext:
On February 13 of this year the Minister of Mines and Resources made a speech over the air. in which he said:
One of the most noteworthy features of the rehabilitation program is the reawakening of interest in Indian arts and crafts.
Further on he stated:
It is the intention of the department to encourage production of only high quality materials and to assure, wherever possible, continuity of supply. An attempt is being made to open up markets where these products can be sold at a reasonable price, but nevertheless a price that will encourage the Indian to excel in his craftsmanship.

Supply-Mines-Indian Affairs
This year in the debate on the budget I exhibited two totem poles, and brought them to the attention of the house, but I believe on that occasion the minister was unavoidably absent. To-night I should like to tell him what is taking place in British Columbia. In my right hand I show him a totem pole carved by an Indian in North Vancouver. In my left hand I hold a totem pole marked "made in Japan," and it has not even the likeness of an Indian, but rather that of a Mongolian. But visitors from the United States and elsewhere who are looking for Indian craftsmanship have the Japanese article foisted on them as being an Indian totem pole.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Is it marked "made in Japan"?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Yes. The Japanese article, of course, has no connection with any Indian craft, and does not compare at all favourably with the one made by the Indians. This is a craft which belongs to the Indians of North America, and no country should be permitted to take an advantage of this kind. I thought the procedure was patented, but I am taking this opportunity of bringing the matter to the attention of the minister. The Japanese article should not be allowed to come into the country and be sold as an Indian totem pole. It has no resemblance to the real article, but is palmed off on those who do not know, and it is sold at practically the same price.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Has anything been done to patent Indian craftsmanship such as that shown by the hon. member for New Westminster?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
No; it might be rather difficult to patent a totem pole. They are made in many different forms in many places by many Indians. I realize the point raised by the hon. member for New Westminster is an important one, and some consideration has been given to it, not only in regard to totem poles but in regard to other classes of Indian handicraft work. The Japanese have placed quantities of articles on the Canadian market, and, I assume, on the markets of other countries. I think under our law it is necessary that they indicate on their goods the country of origin, but the purchaser does not always examine closely enough to see whether or not it is a genuine piece of Indian handicraft or an imitation. I do not know what could be done, short of putting a ban on those imports, and perhaps that would be a rather serious step to take. So long as articles are clearly marked "made in Japan," 71492-296
the purchaser must be aware that he is buying not the genuine Indian handicraft but a spurious article made in a foreign country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The trouble is that the mark is very small. One can scarcely see it, and many visitors do not think of looking for it. They ask if it is an Indian totem pole, and when they are told that it is they buy it as such. There is no use in encouraging the making of these totem poles so long as the Japanese article is permitted to compete. Through this competition the Indians are deprived of part of their livelihood, and I would ask the minister to look into the matter in order to see what can be done to prevent the sale of these importations.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The matter has been and is under consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: It strikes me that the handicraft work of Indians in Canada could be copyrighted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Frankly, I think it could be. Certainly it is worth while studying the matter and making the strongest possible effort to enforce copyright restrictions. But if that is not possible I think parliament should not hesitate definitely to prohibit the importation of alleged copies of Indian handicraft work. Those of us who live in British Columbia are well acquainted with the history and stories of the totem pole. Those stories and the totem poles are peculiar to the Indians; they are not created out of fancy, but are of long standing and of great historical value. I suggest that the department should take up the question of copyrighting not only totem poles but other handicraft work of the Indians, not only in British Columbia but in other parts of Canada as well. If that cannot be done, then I certainly suggest that we should prohibit the importation of articles which are obviously spurious copies of Indian handicraft.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The difficulty arises only in British Columbia, so far as Japanese competition is concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Which makes it all the more simple, and all the more emphatic.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT

I should like to support my colleague with regard to this matter. The same observations would apply to the work of the Indians in the Georgian bay and Timagami districts. When one goes to Gravenhurst, or to the various points in that district, he finds the country flooded with souvenirs, consisting of baskets and articles of that kind, and if a person were to

Supply-Mines-Indian Affairs

look close enough he would find on a bottom corner "made in UJ3A." We must remember that this provides one of the livelihoods of our Indians. As I said before, they contribute a great deal toward attracting tourist trade by their colourfulness, and I cannot understand why they should have to meet this competition. We should do everything in our power to protect the production of these tourist souvenirs. We talk about the value to Canada of our tourist trade, but I often wonder how much that trade is worth when United States visitors come to Canada and buy souvenirs with the words "made in the United States" or something else on the bottom. Sometimes the article is made in the United States, but is not marked. If we are going to conserve the benefits of our tourist trade for the people of this country and for our Indians, we should see that they have the opportunity of making these articles.

speechtext:
I should like to
associate myself definitely with the remarks of the last three hon. gentlemen. There is an Indian reservation in my constituency, and I can remember when I was a small boy that the Indians had the ability to do i*emarkable bits of work. They seem to be losing that ability to a large extent, and I was wondering whether any effort was being made in the Indian schools to develop among the Indian youth that ability which their fathers used to have in the manufacturing of handicraft articles.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I will deal with that question under the next item.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: We should absolutely prohibit the importation of imitation Indian goods. Our Indians can supply the needs of the tourists. I know if I were a tourist and visited a country in which there were Indians, if I purchased a piece of what I supposed was Indian work and found that it had been made in Japan or in some other country I would not feel so kindly disposed toward the country which permitted that to take place. It would be an attraction to tourists if they were assured that the Indian articles they purchased were really made by them.

speechtext:
Under this and the next item there is an expenditure of approximately $2,000,000 for education. The other evening when I heard over the radio one of our Indian chiefs addressing Their Majesties the King and Queen at Calgary, I was struck with the excellent English vocabulary he had,

a vocabulary which would have done credit to any English-speaking person. I have often wondered why more of our Indian children do not receive better educations. A couple of years ago I visited the Indian school at Duncan, British Columbia. This is a mixed school presided over by a young lady. I do not think it was a denominational school, but the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) will know. I know something of school work; I looked over the work being done in this school quite carefully, and in my opinion the Indian children compared quite well with children in the same grades in an English-speaking country school.
What facilities are provided to permit Indian children to go beyond the grade schools? What encouragement is given them to continue with their high school work and perhaps prepare themselves to go back among the Indians and lead them toward that kind of life which perhaps they would lead in a more civilized society? I notice in looking over the details of this item that the bulk of the expenditures is for the residential schools and I see from the details that there are two inspectors of Indian schools, one at $2,460 and one at $600 for part-time services. Are these the only inspectional services provided? With the number of schools and the great distances that separate them, it would seem to me that this inspection service would be entirely inadequate to meet our needs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
With the exception of British Columbia and New Brunswick, I believe I am correct in saying that the inspection of Indian schools is carried out by the inspectors of the departments of education in the various provinces. I think the work of inspection is fairly well provided for in that way.
Perhaps I may say a word or two now in regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). When one is dealing with the question of education one is dealing with something in connection with which difficulties may readily arise. I think it is a fair statement to say that education among the Indians had its genesis in the missionary efforts toward Christianizing the Indians which were made many years ago. It quickly became apparent to the missionaries of all religious denominations that if any progress were to be made, a different environment would have to be thrown round the Indians. This led to the development of residential schools which under the circumstances largely became church schools aided

Supply-Mines-Indian Affairs
by the state. In. many instances the state built the school; in others it assisted in the building, and in others the church built the school. In all instances the residential schools are operated with a grant from the federal government on the basis of pupil enrolment to assist in carrying on the work of education. In addition to the residential schools, there is a large number of day schools. For the information of the committee I may say that there are in operation in Canada eighty residential schools and 277 day schools. I can give the information by provinces if it is required.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: It is all in the reports.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Trends in modern education have been fairly well marked within the last decade or two. I think educationalists have improved methods; at any rate, they t'hink they have, and I daresay they are right. There has been an improvement in educational matters, not only in our universities but in our public and day schools, and the same thing applies to our Indian schools.
My acquaintance with the department and my observation have led me pretty definitely to the conclusion that sufficient emphasis was not placed upon the vocational training of the Indian children. The problem arose, and it arises to-day, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport a short time ago. Indian children, at the age of five or six years, are brought in to the residential schools, very often quite a distance from the reserves where their parents live, and they stay in residence because the school desires to keep them until they are at least fifteen or sixteen years of age. The purpose was to keep the children removed for as long a period as possible from the influences of the reserve, often remote, on which they had been born and lived until they came into the residential school. It has not always, I am bound to say, worked out well. An Indian lad or an Indian girl stays in the residential school until sixteen or seventeen or eighteen years of age.
When they leave school the only place for the great majority of them to go is back to the reserves from which they were taken at the age of five or six or seven. Very often it was found that they were unable to apply on the reserve the knowledge they had obtained in the schools, and during the period from six to sixteen or seventeen years in which they had been away from the reserve they had lost the opportunity of acquiring some of the arts, crude as they may have been, which their parents practised on the reserve and in their daily vocations. So, while 71492-2941
one finds some of the older women on the reserves, particularly in the northern parts of the provinces, highly skilled in certain classes of needlework, bead work and the like, these arts have largely been lost to the youngsters who have passed through the residential schools. As a result there is an increasing recognition to-day among all the churches- and I cannot praise the efforts of the churches too highly-of the need of giving direction to the activities of the school in the way of vocational training. As a consequence the boys in the residential schools are more and more being provided with the opportunity of becoming acquainted, for instance, with the operation of an outboard motor on a canoe, and of learning something about the gasoline engine of an outboard motor, knowledge which can be put to practical use when the lad leaves school and goes in for hunting or trapping or whatever his vocation may be. That is something of practical value.
The development of handicraft, art, skill in weaving and the like among the girls has also been marked in some of the residential schools. It is the intention of the department, I may say to the hon. member for New Westminster, to encourage that in every way possible. Some of the Indians have shown remarkable skill in handicraft work and they can be wisely assisted in improving their technique in these arts. Recently we have opened up a branch of the department which supplies these raw materials to many of the Indian girls and boys, and undertakes to market the products of their skill. While it is early yet to reach any definite conclusion, I think a definite field of usefulness is opening up in that direction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I agree with the minister that we should encourage vocational training of the Indian boys and girls. Is any provision made for the Indian boy or girl who shows particular aptitude as a scholar continuing to higher education?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: How many are taken beyond the public school grade?

There is one matter
which should be discussed. I do not know whether it comes under this item or not. Has the department taken any steps to make up to the Indians what they have lost because of their inability to find seasonal employment? There was a time, ten or fifteen years ago, when at almost any time in the spring or fall Indians could go off their reservation and find work such as, in my constituency, beet work and picking up potatoes. Nowadays it is almost impossible for the Indians to get that work. At the same time, so far as I am informed, no extra allowance because of that condition is being made to the Indians. The result is that those on the reservation in my constituency are in really a bad way economically. Has the minister thought about that matter and has anything been done?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT

I would suppose that the situation applied throughout the country.
Here is another illustration. An Indian used to be able to go in the harvest field and make a fair amount of money by stooking grain, hauling, threshing, and that sort of thing. The coming in of the combine has virtually eliminated all that work; and the anxiety of whites to get work in the beet fields, the potato fields and in any other kind of seasonal employment there may happen to be has filled the field so far as the Indians are concerned. The result is that they are much hampered in trying to make a living, and they are suffering just as much as.are the whites from the low prices of cattle and other products which they produce. To-day they are in a serious plight, to which we have probably not given sufficient attention. Has the matter been brought to the notice of the minister?

To follow this up a little, some years ago the Indians who raised cattle were sure of a profitable market. The same was true of those who raised horses, and in my constituency they used to raise them in great numbers. Everyone knows that to-day there is nothing in the raising of horses, and as for cattle, one cannot sell them for as much as they cost to produce. The result is that the Indians are seriously handicapped.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That particular reserve is agricultural. The total quantity of all grains produced on the reserve last year, I am informed by the deputy, was around 250,000 bushels. It also carries a considerable number of live stock-horses and cattle. It is quite true that the Indians there are agriculturists; and while they may not be farming as successfully as some of their white compatriots, they are making good progress. During the period of low prices of agricultural products they have suffered as other agricultural communities have suffered, but I am not aware there is any hardship on the reserve. So far as the future is concerned, it appears to me that the solution in respect of that reserve is to develop grain growing, stock raising and the like. I believe there is some reason for expecting that the Indians there will make steady progress in that direction. In many, many instances they are doing very well.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
This work was started a few years ago looking to the restoration of fur bearing animals in the northern parts of our provinces. For the information of the committee I may say that approximately one-third of the Indian population of Canada are known as hunting and trapping Indians, who live by the chase, These Indians are located in the northern parts of the various provinces. Unfortunately the lack of sound conservation methods in the past has resulted in a great depletion of the fur bearing animals, with the inevitable result that the natural mode of living of these Indians has largely vanished, and in increasing numbers they are coming upon public relief. We have endeavoured to make arrangements with the provinces, with success in several instances, to have areas set aside where we would undertake the work, for example, of putting in dams,
Vegetable Oils

or taking the necessary steps to recreate the natural conditions under which fur bearers, particularly muskrat, will propagate. Part of this vote will be spent in Manitoba, part in Saskatchewan, part in Alberta and a small amount in Quebec.
